body: When a trial has more than two possible outcomes which are all equally likely to happen, each outcome has less than an even chance of happening. E.g. each number on a dice has the same likelihood of being rolled, but each is less than an even chance.

body: Folk music encompasses many traditions from around the world that have been passed through generations orally.

title: Folk music all sounds the same.
body: Many folk traditions have shared characteristics, primarily because of the way that the music was passed between generations, but folk music is incredibly diverse, and covers lots of different types of music from different cultures and times.

body: The melodies usually have a small range and are conjunct, which makes them easier to sing and memorise.

title: You can fit any lyrics to a melody.

title: Sea shanties are songs for pirates.
body: Many cultures based around the sea use songs to coordinate movement on boats. Sea shanties are one example of this, and were sung by many, including sailors and fishermen. Other traditional cultures had their own songs for this purpose.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many folk music traditions use music for dance, including for celebrations like marriages and harvest.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Like most dance music, folk dance needs a clear pulse, suitable tempo and repeated rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Korobeiniki is a Russian folk song often used for dancing, that was famously used for the video game Tetris.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It includes four-bar phrases, dotted crotchets and it is based on a minor scale.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The music repeats and uses repeat marks in the notation to show this.

title: Hand positions should only change at the start of new phrases.
body: This depends entirely on what notes are used. Sometimes, like in Korobeiniki, it is more useful to change hand position during a phrase. When doing this, we should always practise making it seamless, so there is no obvious change in sound.

body: Folk dances often have highly rhythmic accompaniment parts which make them effective for dancing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These will often use repeated rhythms that create rhythmic drive, which is a feeling of energy.

body: In Korobeiniki, we can create a simple accompaniment using the bass notes A, D and E.

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The human voice can only produce one note at a time.
body: Every sound we make has multiple different notes, its just that the main note is much louder than the others. Think about when you have a croaky voice - it almost sounds like multiple notes, because it is! Multiphonics just amplify the quieter notes.

body: Composers have used recordings of sound in their music since recording technology was created.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This ranges from abstract-sounding musique concrète, to using samples of sound and music in popular music styles.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Sampling is the process of creating samples - clips of pre-existing sound or music that are used in a new way.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To create samples, we isolate individual sounds.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can then combine them in a new way to create a musical pattern.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Samples are always non-musical sounds.
body: This is not true - a sample is any pre-existing sound that is used in a new way. This could be traditionally non-musical sounds like machinery or speech, or it could be clips of pieces of music or individual notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pitched sounds, such as musical notes, vocals or buzzing machines can be sampled.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These can create unique timbres and textures, particularly when they are altered and recombined.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can alter them in many ways, including changing the pitch and adding effects.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By experimenting with different patterns of pitched samples, we can create unique hooks and riffs.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Only musical instruments (and voices) produce pitched sound.
body: Pitched sounds are everywhere. In fact, most sounds have a pitch, it is often just hard to hear it. You can probably hear a pitched sound now if you listen closely - electrical buzzing, distant speech, weather or animals all produce subtle pitches.

body: Serialism developed in the 20th century, with composers searching for a new approach to composition.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is atonal, meaning that it has no key or tonic note.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Everything in a piece is based on a unique tone row - the 12 notes of the chromatic scale arranged in a specific order.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A tone row must use all 12 notes and avoid repeating any.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Arnold Schoenberg and Elisabeth Lutyens are two well-known serialist composers.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: atonal
body: music which has no key or tonic note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: serialism
body: an atonal composition method based on a specific order of pitches (a tone row)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tone row

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chromatic scale

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A tone row is just a scale.
body: A tone row is different because it isn't just a set of notes to choose from, but a specific order. When you are composing something in C major, you can use the notes of the C major scale in any order. With a tone row, they have a specific order.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Serialist composers use tone rows in many different ways.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This includes varying the timbre, instrument, rhythm, dynamics, octave and articulation.

body: As long as the order of the pitches doesn’t change, this is considered ‘within the rules’ of serialism.

title: Retrograding breaks the rules of serialism because it changes the order of the notes.
body: Serialist composers don't consider retrograding breaking the rules. It does change the order, but the new order is still closely linked to the original tone row (by being reversed). It is therefore an acceptable and musically interesting technique.

body: In EDM the texture can vary between thick and thin to create excitement and interest.

body: A ground bass is a short, repeated bass line that repeats throughout a piece, forming the structure of the music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ground bass was popular in baroque music but repeated chord sequences are still common in today's pop music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A ground bass tends to start on the tonic note to reinforce the key.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A ground bass finishes on the dominant or leading note which naturally wants to return to the tonic note to start again.

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A ground bass pattern should finish on the tonic as it 'sounds' finished.
body: The final bar of the piece should finish on the tonic note, but until that bar, the pattern wants to repeat. Finishing on the dominant or the leading note naturally helps the music return to the first note of the pattern, which should be the tonic.

title: An interval of a 3rd is three tones higher or lower than the first note.
body: In C major (where pupils are counting the white keys), they should count the starting note and final note, plus any in between. So an interval of a 3rd is actually two tones higher or lower than the first note. An octave would be seven notes higher.

body: Some of the most popular phrase structures that achieve this balance are AABB, AABA, ABAB and ABAC.

title: Not everyone can write a good melody.
body: Writing a melody is just like writing a paragraph. Break it into small chunks (phrases). If you are finding it difficult to create a phrase, keep it simple and start by just improvising using 2 or 3 notes.

body: Songwriters create musical contrast by making sections or musical ideas sound different from each other.

body: This is exaggerated in grunge, reflecting the emotional lyrics.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can create contrast through considered use of dynamics, timbre, pitch, texture, rhythm and harmonic rhythm.

body: The middle 8 is a contrasting section, usually 8 bars long, heard in the second half of a song.

title: Musical contrast
body: When there are differences between sections we would describe this as musical contrast.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Middle 8
body: The middle 8 is a section in a song that contrasts with the verse and the chorus. It is often 8 bars long.

title: Harmonic rhythm
body: Harmonic rhythm is how often the chords change.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Harmonic rhythm means the rhythm that each chord plays.
body: Harmonic rhythm means how often the chords change, not the actual rhythm that the chords play. Show examples of the same harmonic rhythm different rhythms in the chords. Changing the harmonic rhythm is a useful tool to alter the feel of music.

body: The intro and outro are important parts of a structure - they provide the 'frame' for the main content of the song.

body: The intro and outro are usually based on musical ideas from the verse or chorus.

body: The intro is an opportunity to introduce some of the musical ideas and set the mood for the song.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The outro provides a neat ending to the song. It is not used in all songs.

title: Outro

body: Film music can be used in a variety of ways to shape our experience.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These include setting the scene, creating tension, and use of leitmotif to represent a particular character or idea.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers use the musical elements to create an appropriate atmosphere, including appropriate use of tonality.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Title themes are often the first music in a film, so should set the tone for the whole film.

body: The silent movie era was between the 1890s and 1920s.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In this period, film music was performed live by a solo performer (often improvised) or a group.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The performers tried to capture and exaggerate the mood of scenes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Chase scenes were common in silent movies.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The music often used a fast tempo, fast rhythms and scalic runs to create a sense of excitement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Music for films is always recorded and played through speakers.
body: Before technology existed to do this, film music was played live by performers in the room. It would often be a solo piano/organ player, who would improvise along with the film. Sometimes, ensembles such as orchestras would play music live instead.

body: Mickey-mousing is a common technique in early movies.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This is where the music copies the movement of a character.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many early movies also involve scenes in which music is key to creating suspense.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Typical suspenseful music uses dissonant chords (such as diminished sevenths) and sudden changes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: mickey-mousing

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A diminished seventh chord is just like any other extended chord - a triad with added notes.
body: A diminished seventh chord is quite unique as every interval is the same size (three semitones). It is different from extended chords that add notes to a triad. It has been used for centuries as a tense, dramatic chord, including in silent movies.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Music in silent movies has to transition seamlessly between different scenes and moods.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many performers played popular songs and used musical clichés in their musical performances.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: One famous example is the ‘misterioso’ musical cliché.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To transition between scenes, performers often played a vamp, a repeated pattern based on chords.

title: When a piano player plays music with a silent movie it is always completely improvised.
body: While they improvise many aspects, they often use specific musical ideas to create specific effects. This includes vamps, certain chords (e.g. diminished 7th for tension) and musical clichés like the misterioso that create certain effects.

body: Leitmotifs are musical ideas that represent ideas, characters or places.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They were used in opera and became popular in films after the end of silent movies in the 1920s.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers capture the important features of a character in a leitmotif to support the audience’s understanding of them.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They do this by choosing suitable keys, pitch and rhythms, including the use of strong rhythms for powerful characters.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By changing a leitmotif, a composer can reflect changes in that character or in the plot.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: leitmotif
body: a short musical idea that represents a character, place or idea
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: opera
body: a form of storytelling using dramatic singing, acting, costume and design and sometimes dance
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: strong rhythms
body: rhythms which accent the strong beat (beat 1 in the bar) or mainly land on the beat; they are predictable and repetitive
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A leitmotif and a film theme are the same thing.
body: Not quite. Many films have themes that represent the overall mood, and can be heard throughout the film. The difference with a leitmotif is that it explicitly represents one thing - a character, place or an idea.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers use leitmotif to tell us about a character or idea, but also to show changes that occur.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This is done through motivic transformation - changing aspects of the leitmotif to represent changes in the character.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can change most aspects of a leitmotif, but must keep the melodic shape similar so that it is still recognisable.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Changing articulation, rhythms, dynamics, tempo and harmony can transform a leitmotif to create very different emotions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: leitmotif
body: a short musical idea that represents a character, place or idea
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: motivic transformation
body: when a motif is changed to represent a change in a story or character
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melodic shape
body: the overall shape of a melody or part of a melody, including where it ascends or descends and where it is conjunct or disjunct
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Simply changing the instrument makes a leitmotif change mood.
body: While it does have an impact, changing other elements can make this even greater. Harmony, rhythm, dynamics, articulation and tempo are particularly useful for motivic transformation.

title: Reggaeton

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Dembow beat
body: The dembow beat is the typical drum groove heard in reggaeton music, which uses the tresillo rhythm and has a strong beat on the kick drum.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The tresillo ('triplet' in Spanish) uses three equally spaced notes.
body: The notes in the tresillo rhythm are not equally spaced. The third note is a shorter duration. Counting the semiquavers in a 3-3-2 pattern can help us space the notes correctly (1-2-3, 1-2-3, 1-2).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Reggaeton has evolved from being popular in Puerto Rico to being a globally successful genre.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It has influenced many pop artists, including Ed Sheeran, Clean Bandit and Dua Lipa.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When different musical styles are combined, such as using the dembow beat in pop music, it results in a musical fusion.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can create more complex variations on the dembow beat by adding timbales, extra percussion and drum rolls.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Timbales

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: It is important to constantly create variety and change in a composition.

body: a low-pitched part that supports the harmony and melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: timbre
body: the description of the sound or tone of an instrument
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Only highly skilled and naturally gifted musicians can work out music by ear.
body: Anyone can work out music by ear. It just takes practice and is made easier through use of effective strategies, including working out rhythm and pitch separately, and identifying individual pitches through trial and error.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Drum beats can be recreated by ear by using similar techniques to working out a melodic line.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Breaking it into small chunks and trying to pick out individual instruments or lines helps.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Blinding Lights has a typical pop drum groove, with a snare backbeat, repeated hi-hats and kick emphasising 1 and 3.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The hook uses a synth lead and has syncopated rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: hook
body: a memorable, repeated musical idea
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: synth lead
body: a type of synthesised sound that is suited to playing melodies
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Syncopated
body: a rhythm that emphasises (accents) notes in between the main beats; this is often created by using half-beat rests on the beat or dotted rhythms
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: All drum grooves have exactly the same rhythms in the kick, snare and hi-hat.
body: Many typical drum grooves do have the same features or features very close to this, however encourage pupils to identify where there are subtle differences and how the kick, snare and hi-hat patterns can be varied within these features.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Identifying repeated phrases can make it easier to recreate melodic ideas quickly.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The hook in As It Was uses two repeated phrases that are only slightly different from each other.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Accompaniments often use synth pads, which are effective for sustained notes and chords.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Identifying the melodic shape of a pattern can help to accurately work out the notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accompaniment
body: a part in the music that supports the melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Phrase
body: a short section of a melody, often lasting 1, 2 or 4 bars
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: synth pad
body: a type of synthesised sound that is suited to playing sustained sounds
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melodic shape
body: the overall shape of a melody or part of a melody, including where it ascends or descends and where it is conjunct or disjunct
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Synthesisers are most effective for melodic lines.
body: Different types of synthesiser suit different musical roles. While synth leads are very effective for melodic lines, synth pads are well-suited to playing accompaniments, particularly sustained notes and chords.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Bass guitarists in pop and rock styles often work out iconic bass riffs to help develop their skills.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The bass riff in Under Pressure is very famous and creates a pedal by repeating the same pitches as the chords change.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The bass riff in Feel Good Inc. is more complex as it is syncopated and has more varied pitches.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To work out a bass riff, the key is to hear it on its own, break it into small chunks and work out notes one-by-one.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: riff
body: a short, repeated musical phrase or pattern
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pedal
body: a continuous pitch or note in the music which remains the same as the other harmonies change
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: interval
body: the distance in pitch between two notes (e.g. a fifth)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Bass parts are normally simple and just play the lowest notes from the chords.
body: In some cases this is true, but in many cases bass lines are interesting patterns and can often be defining features of songs. This is true for both Under Pressure and Feel Good Inc.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Chord vi is the relative minor chord in a major key.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It can be used to briefly suggest minor tonality, adding complexity and interest to a chord sequence.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The bass part is crucial to harmony, because it emphasises key notes in each chord and determines chord inversions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is usually notated in bass clef.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using the bass to emphasise root position chords helps to strengthen the harmony.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: relative minor
body: the minor chord or key that has the same key signature as a major key (e.g. A minor compared to C major)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonic
body: chord I - the 'home' note and chord of a key and the note that the key is named after
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dominant
body: the fifth note in a scale, or the chord based on that note (chord V)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: root position
body: a chord in which the root note is the lowest note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chord inversion
body: when the notes of a chord are reordered so that the root is not the lowest note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: You should use root position chords sparingly because they sound uninteresting.
body: Not necessarily. Root position chords are important because they anchor the music in the key. Most chords in a chord sequence should be root position, with some inversions used to add interst and variety.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Melodies that use disjunct movement can be very effective, if disjunct intervals are used carefully.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In particular, 3rds, 5ths and octaves tend to be most effective.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Any disjunct movement should jump between chord tones.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Balanced phrasing is a key feature of Western classical melodies.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: With this, phrases are an equal length and use a 'question' and 'answer' form with a similar rhythm and melodic shape.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: interval
body: the distance in pitch between two notes (e.g. a fifth)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chord tone
body: a note that is included within a chord
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: disjunct
body: movement between notes that involves intervals larger than two semitones (moving by leap)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: balanced phrasing
body: where melodic phrases are equal length and complementary melodic shape (also called 'question and answer' form)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melodic shape
body: the overall shape of a melody or part of a melody, including where it ascends or descends and where it is conjunct or disjunct
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Only 3rds, 5ths and octaves work as disjunct intervals in a melody.
body: This is not true: all intervals (except sevenths) can work effectively, as long as they jump between chord tones. If intervals jump to or from non-chord tones, the melody will sound ineffective.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A typical 16-bar classical melody has a contrasting section of harmony and melody in bars 9-12.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This usually ends with chord V, creating an imperfect cadence.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The melody and harmony in bar 13-16 typically copy bar 5-8, ending with a perfect cadence.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An anacrusis is an interesting melodic feature that can help to make a melody sound more unique and interesting.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonic
body: chord I - the 'home' note and chord of a key and the note that the key is named after
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dominant
body: the fifth note in a scale, or the chord based on that note (chord V)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: imperfect cadence
body: where part of a chord sequence finishes on the dominant chord (V), which feels unfinished
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: anacrusis
body: when a melody starts before the downbeat (beat 1)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: There are no 'rules' for writing a chord sequence.
body: While to some extent this is true, in Western classical music there are very typical patterns that are used very regularly. These include the position of perfect and imperfect cadences, and what the chords do throughout the 16 bars.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When arranging a composition for an ensemble we must consider the strengths of the instruments in the ensemble.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This includes instrument ranges and possible techniques (such as pizzicato).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In a string quartet, the first violin normally plays the melody and the cello plays the bass part.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The second violin and viola play harmony, splitting the remaining chord tones between them.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To arrange chords, consider voicing, move by small intervals, and make sure all chord tones are played in each chord.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: string quartet
body: a common western classical ensemble consisting of two violins, a viola and a cello
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: harmony
body: how different notes and chords work together
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: range
body: the range of pitches that an instrument is capable of playing
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: voicing
body: how the notes in a chord are spread out on an instrument or between instruments
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pizzicato
body: a string technique in which the performer plucks the string with a finger
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: As long as the chord tones in the chord are played, it doesn't matter how these notes are split between the 2nd violin and viola.
body: This does matter. The voicing of the chord makes a big difference to how it sounds. Avoiding large intervals between those instruments, and making sure that the chords aren't very low or high pitched makes them sound effective.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adding countermelodies and developing texture are effective ways to develop an ensemble composition.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A countermelody is a second and equally prominent melody that plays at the same time as the main melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In a string quartet, the second violin or viola normally play countermelodies, although sometimes the cello does.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When adding countermelodies or developing texture it is crucial to make sure that every part can still be heard well.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The chord tones of each chord should still be played across all parts to ensure the harmony is still effective.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: string quartet
body: a common western classical ensemble consisting of two violins, a viola and a cello
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: countermelody
body: a second melody that plays at the same time as the main melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: texture
body: how something feels when it is touched
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melody and accompaniment
body: a texture consisting of a melody with a clearly separate accompaniment
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A countermelody is just a type of accompaniment.
body: It is actually quite different from an accompaniment, because it should be equally as prominent as the main melody, whereas an accompaniment is not. An accompaniment is usually also based on repeating patterns, whereas a melody does not have to be.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know how to read the treble clef
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know that music often has a melody and an accompaniment
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have experience improvising new melodic ideas
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Effective melodies balance repetition and contrast.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They are built using the notes of a particular scale and a variety of rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using 2-bar phrases and conjunct movement helps a melody to sound effective.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Melodies use the dominant (fifth) halfway through to sound unfinished, then the tonic at the end to sound finished.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is possible to write effective melodies without all of these rules, but they are a good starting point for composing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Melody
body: the tune, usually the most memorable feature in a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Scale
body: a set of notes
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Conjunct
body: movement between notes based on small intervals (steps)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Phrase
body: a short section of a melody, often lasting 1, 2 or 4 bars
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonic
body: chord I - the 'home' note and chord of a key and the note that the key is named after
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Using new ideas in every bar is the best way to compose a melody
body: Finding a balance of repetition and variety is usually more successful as it helps the melody become memorable.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers use motifs, short melodic ideas that are repeated, to give melodies a sense of coherence and unity.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Motifs don’t need to be repeated exactly every time, but they need to sound familiar to the listener.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Sequences are an effective melodic device for extending a melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They help to maintain a balance between familiarity and contrast.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: motif
body: a short melodic idea that recurs throughout a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: coherence
body: the quality of forming a unified whole
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sequence
body: a short melodic idea that is repeated in steps either rising or falling
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A melody must feature a motif.
body: This is not necessarily true - great melodies do not have to use motifs. However, they are a useful feature to understand when learning to write melodies, because they encourage composers to balance repetition anc contrast effectively.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Chord sequences are patterns of chords that form the harmony in a composition.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Starting on chord I (tonic) and using mostly primary chords (chords I, IV and V) helps to anchor the music in a key.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using some secondary chords (ii, iii and vi) adds further interest, but these should be used sparingly.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ending with a perfect cadence (chord V to I) helps the music feel finished.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using an imperfect cadence (any chord to V) in the middle of the sequence (bar 4) helps the music sound unfinished.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Primary chord
body: the most useful chords in a key - chord I (1), IV (4) and V (5)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Secondary chord
body: chords ii (2), iii (3) and vi (6) in a key
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonic
body: chord I - the 'home' note and chord of a key and the note that the key is named after
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Perfect cadence
body: a V-I progression at the end of a section of music; it feels resolved
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: imperfect cadence
body: where part of a chord sequence finishes on the dominant chord (V), which feels unfinished
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Secondary chords shouldn't be used.
body: Secondary chords are important for interesting harmony and using them is a good idea. As you become a more experienced composer, you'll learn how to effectively use them. For now, a good rule of thumb is to use them sparingly.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Chord inversions and broken chords can add interest to a chord sequence without changing the harmony.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Chord inversions change the root position triad so the root note is no longer the lowest note in the chord.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using chord inversions can make chord sequences easier to play and sound more melodic.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Broken chords can add rhythmic interest to a chord sequence.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chord inversion
body: when the notes of a chord are reordered so that the root is not the lowest note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Triad
body: A triad is a chord made up of three notes from the scale: the root, third and fifth.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: root note
body: the main note of a chord, and what the chord is named after
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: root position
body: a chord in which the root note is the lowest note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: broken chord
body: when the notes of a chord are sounded one at a time
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Using chord inversions for every chord will make the chord sequence more interesting.
body: Using some inversions can make the chord sequence more interesting, but too many can sound unusual. Starting and finishing with a root position chord can help to reinforce the key.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Melody and harmony must use some of the same notes to sound musically coherent.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Chord tones should form the basis of a melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Passing notes can make a melody interesting and more ‘melodic’ by creating conjunct movement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Melodies should still follow a recognisable or repeated phrase pattern.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chord tone
body: a note that is included within a chord
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: phrases
body: a short section of a melody, often lasting 1, 2 or 4 bars
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: passing notes
body: a non-chord tone that links two chord tones by step
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Conjunct
body: movement between notes based on small intervals (steps)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A melody must be completely conjunct.
body: This is not true - great melodies often use disjunct movement. However, when learning to compose melodies, sticking to mostly conjunct movement and small intervals helps them to sound melodic.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A broad understanding of key differences between the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An understanding of the orchestra and its development
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An understanding of treble clef notation
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An understanding of meanings of the core musical elements
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An understanding of small ensembles and key genres across the Western Classical Tradition.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Baroque music has certain distinctive characteristics.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These include use of continuo, terraced dynamics and contrapuntal textures.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Melodies are often long and flowing and are decorated with ornamentation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Key genres include the trio sonata, suite, prelude and fugue, concerto and overture.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Baroque period
body: the period of Western classical music between 1600 and 1750
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: continuo
body: the accompaniment section of the Baroque orchestra, normally including harpsichord and a bass stringed instrument (e.g. cello)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ornamentation
body: when a performer decorates a melody with extra notes (e.g. trills, turns)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: terraced dynamics
body: where dynamics change suddenly, rather than gradually
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: contrapuntal
body: a type of polyphonic texture that includes two or more interweaving melodic lines
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: All Baroque music is contrapuntal / polyphonic.
body: Textures are varied in the Baroque period, but use of contrapuntal/polyphonic textures was very common and contrasts with the later Classical period. This is a typical texture of the period, but not the only one.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Music from the Classical period (1750-1820) has certain defining characteristics.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These include melody and accompaniment texture, and simple melodies with limited ornamentation and balanced phrasing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The orchestra grew larger and, as well as the concerto, the symphony became a key genre. It has four movements.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The first uses sonata form, with an exposition, development and recapitulation. The third is often a minuet and trio.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The sonata became a key genre (particularly for keyboard instruments), with three contrasting movements.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Classical period
body: the period of Western classical music between 1750 and 1820
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: symphony
body: a long composition for orchestra, usually consisting of four shorter pieces (movements)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sonata
body: a three-movement solo composition, and a structure with exposition, development and recapitulation
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: balanced phrasing
body: where melodic phrases are equal length and complementary melodic shape (also called 'question and answer' form)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Sonata form and a sonata are the same thing.
body: This is a common misconception. Sonata form is a structure in a piece that has a exposition, development and recapitulation. A sonata is a three-movement composition for solo instrument. The first movement of a sonata is normally in sonata form.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Romantic period, composers often focused on creating dramatic, emotive and highly expressive music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It used complex chromatic harmony and varied textures, timbres and articulation to create vivid musical moods.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many composers wrote programme music, using techniques like leitmotif to tell stories or evoke images through music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The orchestra became larger and more powerful and, as well as symphonies and concertos, tone poems became a key genre.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The piano was important, with composers like Chopin exploiting its expressive and virtuosic qualities in various genres.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Romantic period
body: the period of Western classical music between roughly 1820 and 1910
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: programme music
body: music that tells a story or creates an image of something
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chromatic
body: a note that is not part of the key or scale
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: leitmotif
body: a short musical idea that represents a character, place or idea
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: virtuosic
body: music that shows off a performer’s technical skill
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Romantic music is related to love and romance.
body: This is not the case - the name is not related to that. Romantic composers focused on creating expression, emotion and evocative moods in their music. Sometimes this would have links with love, but not always.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Texture and harmony had similarities and differences across the Baroque, Classical and Romantic eras.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A key Baroque texture is polyphony, while melody and accompaniment dominated the Classical period.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Romantic period, music was mostly melody and accompaniment, but was more varied and often complex.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Baroque and Classical harmony was diatonic and emphasised modulation to closely-related keys.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Romantic harmony was often chromatic and composers experimented with more complex modulations and chords.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polyphonic
body: a texture with more than one equally important melodic line
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melody and accompaniment
body: a texture consisting of a melody with a clearly separate accompaniment
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diatonic
body: music which uses only notes that are based in the key (e.g. C major or F minor)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chromatic
body: a note that is not part of the key or scale
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: modulation
body: a change of key during a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Each period had a single defining texture (e.g. Baroque = polyphonic).
body: There were typical uses of texture for each period. For example, Baroque composers often used polyphonic textures, much more than Classical composers. However, within each period, there were examples of all textures being used and lots of variety.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the 20th century, classical music developed in various different ways.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many composers used non-functional harmony, while some experimented with atonal and microtonal music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Experimental composers challenged core principles of the Western Classical Tradition (e.g. silent music, chance music).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Minimalist composers wrote mostly diatonic music based on repeating ostinati and gradual changes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: atonal
body: music which has no key or tonic note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: minimalist music (minimalism)
body: a style of music that emerged in the 1960s in the USA, defined by its repetition of minimal musical ideas
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: non-functional harmony
body: where chords don’t have their traditional roles (e.g. chord V resolving to I, using mostly primary chords)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: experimental music
body: music that radically challenges what we think of as 'normal' music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ostinato
body: a short, repeating musical idea (plural: ostinati)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Non-functional harmony sounds the same as functional harmony.
body: While some of the chords might be the same, the difference is in the role. In functional harmony, chords have specific roles (e.g. V coming before I to create resolution). In non-functional harmony, any chord can be used whenever the composer wants.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Basic understanding of the instruments of the orchestra
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Basic understanding of key musical elements - texture, tempo, dynamics and rhythm
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Understanding of basic melodic concepts including phrases
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Western Classical Tradition refers to European art music since the Medieval period.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The three key eras are the Baroque (1600-1750), Classical (1750-1820) and Romantic (1820-1910) periods.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Baroque period used a small orchestra with harpsichord and ornamented melodies. Bach was a key composer.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Classical composers (e.g. Mozart) began to use the piano and most music had a clear melody and accompaniment.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Romantic period music became much more complex, dramatic and emotive. Tchaikovsky was a famous composer.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Western Classical Tradition
body: formal, notated European art music from the Medieval period to the 21st century
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Baroque
body: a period of music history between 1600 and 1750
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Classical
body: a period of music history between 1750 and 1820
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Romantic
body: a period of music history between 1820 and 1910
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Music from the Romantic period is all about love and romance.
body: The word Romantic in the musical sense has nothing to do with love or romance, this was just the name given to the period. The music was often intense, emotive and dramatic, and might sometimes link to ideas of love, but it was very varied.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Between 1600 and 1910 the number of players and variety of instruments in the orchestra increased dramatically.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Baroque orchestra was mostly strings with a few woodwind or brass instruments and a harpsichord.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Classical orchestra was larger, with more woodwind, brass and percussion and no harpsichord.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The huge Romantic orchestra had large woodwind, brass and percussion sections, giving composers many timbres to exploit.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As the orchestra increased in size, woodwind, brass and percussion took on more important roles.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: orchestra
body: a large ensemble that is central to the Western Classical Tradition, consisting of strings, woodwind, brass and percussion instruments
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: strings
body: instruments with strings that are normally played with a bow, including the violin, viola, cello and double bass
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: woodwind
body: instruments that produce sound through blown air, including the flute, clarinet, oboe and bassoon
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: brass
body: metal instruments with valves or slides that produce sound with air, including the trumpet, trombone, French horn and tuba
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: percussion
body: instruments that produce sound by being struck or hit, including drums, cymbals, xylophones and many others
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The orchestra has only grown through the adding of more of the same instruments.
body: The number of players has increased, but the variety of instruments has also increased. Many different instruments have been added to the orchestra since the 1600s, including brass, woodwind, percussion and keyboard instruments.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Chamber music is music in the Western Classical Tradition written for a small ensemble.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Baroque period the trio sonata was the most common form, featuring two melodic instruments with basso continuo.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Classical period the string quartet was very popular, but many other combinations of instruments were also used.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These included trios, duets, quintets and others.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Compositions for solo instrument (with or without accompaniment) have also been popular throughout the periods.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chamber music
body: music composed for a small ensemble, such as a string quartet
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: string quartet
body: a common western classical ensemble consisting of two violins, a viola and a cello
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: piano trio
body: another common small ensemble, typically consisting of a piano, violin and cello
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: trio sonata
body: a common Baroque style of chamber music, with two melodic instruments and continuo
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: solo
body: a performance by one instrument; sometimes compositions for an instrument with a piano accompaniment are also called a solo
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Most music in the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods was written for an orchestra.
body: Although a lot of the most famous music now is orchestral, it was much more diverse than this - composers wrote for many different ensembles, large and small. These included solo compositions, duets, trios, quartets, quintets and many others.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers have used voices in many different ways.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Solo songs, such as lieder, were particularly common from the Romantic period onwards.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They often used techniques such as word-painting and melisma.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Opera used solo singers, a chorus and orchestra to tell epic stories, using arias and recitative.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Baroque period, oratorios and anthems are two key genres of vocal music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: choir / chorus
body: a group of singers, often including soprano, alto, tenor and bass voices (SATB)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: lied
body: a solo song, most common in the Romantic period, usually with piano accompaniment (plural 'lieder')
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: recitative
body: a vocal style that sounds semi-spoken, often used for dialogue in opera
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: word-painting
body: where a vocal melody reflects the meaning of the words (e.g. a descending melody on the word ‘falls’)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melisma
body: where multiple notes are sung during one syllable of a word
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Oratorios and anthems are essentially the same - they are both religious, with similar musical features.
body: Anthems often are a capella, whereas oratorios always have orchestral accompaniment. Oratorios are long pieces of music, consisting of numerous songs that tell a biblical story. Anthems are shorter songs that are used as part of a Christian service.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods, tonality was almost always major or minor.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Every piece has a key signature, which explains which notes should be used in the given key.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Harmony in all three periods is based on primary chords (I, IV and V), with some use of secondary chords.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Romantic composers experimented more with chord choice and chromatic notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cadences are fundamental to all three periods with perfect and imperfect cadences being the most common.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonality
body: the type of notes and chords that a piece of music is based on (e.g. minor, major, atonal)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: harmony
body: how different notes and chords work together
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: key
body: the specific set of notes that a piece is based on (e.g. C minor)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: key signature
body: which sharps or flats should be used in a particular key, written at the start of each stave
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cadence
body: a combination of two chords at the end of a phrase or section
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Harmony and tonality are the same thing.
body: Tonality is to the type of notes and chords that are used (e.g. major). Harmony is the way the notes and chords are used within that key. Think of tonality as a language (e.g. English) and harmony as the word choice and order in a sentence.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know the pitches on the treble clef
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know that a sequence is a pattern repeated at a higher or lower pitch
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know how to write the main rhythmic values: semibreves, minims, crotchets and quavers
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know that music which proceeds to the neighbour note proceeds 'by step'
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know that music which moves over more than one note proceeds 'by leap'
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupil know that a scale is a series of note moving by step
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know that an arpeggio is a broken chord made of three notes moving by leap
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have experience memorising and audiating a newly heard melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Rhythmic dictation is the process of listening to a rhythm and writing it down using notation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Verbalisation, using words to represent different note values and patterns, is a useful strategy for rhythmic dictation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Words like ‘ta’ (crotchet) and ‘ta di’ (pair of quavers) can help to identify different note values.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We then convert those words into their correct notation symbols.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: rhythmic dictation
body: the process of listening to a rhythm and writing it down
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: verbalise
body: to express with words (for example, verbalising a rhythm is turning a rhythm into words)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: note value
body: how long a note lasts for (for example, a crotchet has a note value of one beat)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Longer note values (like minims) are impossible to verbalise, because the words sound the same as a crotchet.
body: Longer note values are tricky to verbalise. A minim uses one syllable, just like a crotchet. The key is to make sure you count how many beats they last for - that will help you tell the difference between crotchets, minims and longer notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Rhythmic dictation is slightly more complex with syncopated and dotted rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Identifying quaver rests (with ‘rest-di’) is useful for accurately notating syncopated rhythms.
