attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In all time signatures we should make sure that the note values add up to the correct number of beats in a bar.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In compound time, we must carefully count groups of 3 quavers (using ‘1 and a 2 and a’ etc.)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Syncopated
body: a rhythm that emphasises (accents) notes in between the main beats; this is often created by using half-beat rests on the beat or dotted rhythms
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Dotted quaver
body: a note that lasts for three quarters of a beat
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Compound time
body: Compound time is when each beat is divided into three quavers, rather than two (e.g. a 12/8 time signature)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: You can use the same verbalisation in compound time as simple time signatures.
body: This will create problems, because there are 3 quavers in each beat in compound time. The counting method in compound time avoids confusion by ensuring there are three quavers in each beat.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Identifying the shape of a melody is key to melodic dictation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The melodic shape has to account for ascending and descending pitch, as well as conjunct and disjunct movement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: With disjunct intervals, we have to listen carefully to notice whether they are large or small leaps.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can represent melodic shape using a line.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can then approximate the correct pitches by drawing notes in to fit the rough melodic shape.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Melodic dictation
body: the process of listening to a melody and writing it down
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melodic shape
body: the overall shape of a melody or part of a melody, including where it ascends or descends and where it is conjunct or disjunct
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Conjunct
body: movement between notes based on small intervals (steps)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: disjunct
body: movement between notes that involves intervals larger than two semitones (moving by leap)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Only advanced musicians can work out a set of notes by listening to them.
body: Anyone can work out notes by ear, if they practise the correct strategies. Identifying the melodic shape, representing it with a line, then carefully converting it into notes is an effective first step in melodic dictation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Identifying intervals is key to melodic dictation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can use reference melodies to help us identify specific intervals by comparing the interval to the specific melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We also need to consider whether an interval is ascending or descending.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Once we have worked out the interval, we can notate it by drawing it on the stave next to the given starting note.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: interval
body: the distance in pitch between two notes (e.g. a fifth)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Semitone
body: A semitone is the smallest interval in most Western music (e.g. C to C#).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Tone
body: The general mood or feeling of a text.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Singing is only useful for singers.
body: When identifying intervals, singing is incredibly useful, even for those who aren't confident singers. Hearing the intervals back through singing or humming allows us to compare them to the reference melodies. Without this, it is much harder.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Notating a whole melody can be done by breaking it into a series of consecutive intervals.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Identify the melodic shape, then identify the first interval by singing it back and compare it to reference melodies.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Notate the first interval, then repeat for each consecutive interval.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Check your answer by matching it to the melodic shape visually and singing it back.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When given the rhythm, we should be careful to accurately copy it in the notated pitches.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: interval
body: the distance in pitch between two notes (e.g. a fifth)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Semitone
body: A semitone is the smallest interval in most Western music (e.g. C to C#).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Tone
body: The general mood or feeling of a text.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Working out the notes of a whole melody by ear is a very difficult musical skill.
body: While it seems challenging, if you break it down into small steps - individual intervals - it is no more difficult than working out one interval. Take it one step at a time in small chunks and it is completely achievable.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils understand the principles of reading treble and bass clef
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils are familiar with melodic devices and key melodic terminology
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils are familiar with harmonic devices and key harmonic terminology
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils can read rhythmic notation, including syncopated rhythms, dotted rhythms and triplets
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know what the primary chords are and how to form triad chords
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know what a key signature is and can name or identify some key signatures
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils understand what a cadence is and know the names of some different cadence types
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Melodies can be analysed by looking at melodic shape, intervals, repetition and contrast, motifs and phrases.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Most composers develop melodies to create a balance between repetition and contrast.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adding notes and changing rhythms are simple ways to develop a melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Augmentation, diminution and sequences are also common methods for melodic development.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: motif
body: a short melodic idea that recurs throughout a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Phrase
body: a short section of a melody, often lasting 1, 2 or 4 bars
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Augmentation
body: the process of lengthening all of the notes in a melody by the same proportion
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Diminution
body: the process of shortening all of the notes in a melody by the same proportion
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sequence
body: a short melodic idea that is repeated in steps either rising or falling
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: If the notes of a melody are changed, that just makes it a new melody.
body: Changing the notes of a melody does create a new melody, but if it is still recognisable as related to the original, we can consider it a developed version of the melody. If it is unrecognisable, then it is not a development but a totally new melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers use different melodic devices to develop and enhance their melodies.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ornamentation is a common melodic device in many styles.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Common ornaments are trills, grace notes, turns and mordents.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Imitation is a device where a part of a melody is copied in another part immediately or shortly afterwards.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A countermelody is a contrasting second melody. It plays at the same time as the main melody and has equal prominence.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: trill
body: a type of ornamentation based on alternating rapidly between two notes
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: mordent
body: a type of ornamentation that creates the effect of a short trill
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: grace note
body: a very fast note that plays just before a main melodic note: it is sometimes referred to as an acciaccatura
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: imitation
body: a melodic device in which part of the melody is copied immediately in another part
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: countermelody
body: a second melody that plays at the same time as the main melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Imitation and a countermelody are the same thing.
body: They are related, but not the same. Imitation has to include copying part of the melody, normally immediately. A countermelody usually tries to contrast with the main melody so that it can be heard clearly separately.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Tonality determines the notes that are used in a piece of music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Lots of Western music is diatonic or chromatic, while many traditional styles around the world are modal.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Atonal music has no key and microtonal music uses notes from in between the semitones.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Identifying intervals allows musicians to work out musical ideas by ear.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The simplest way to do this is by comparing intervals to reference songs.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diatonic
body: music which uses only notes that are based in the key (e.g. C major or F minor)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: atonal
body: music which has no key or tonic note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: modal
body: music based on a mode, a type of scale different from major and minor scales
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chromatic
body: a note that is not part of the key or scale
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Microtonal
body: If a melody is microtonal it uses notes in between the 12 notes of the Western scale. It uses intervals smaller than a semitone.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: If music has a key, it must be diatonic.
body: Not necessarily. A piece of music can have a key, but use notes from outside of it. This would be chromatic. It could also have a key, but use some microtones as well, meaning it is microtonal.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Major triads, minor triads and extended chords can be identified by listening carefully to the feeling of each chord.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The tonic chord (I) can be identified by the ‘finished’ feeling that it creates.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The dominant (V) and subdominant (IV) chords can be identified by listening for the bass notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can identify cadences by the feeling they create - perfect and plagal feel finished, imperfect and interrupted don’t.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Listening for the bass notes helps to distinguish between perfect (V-I) and plagal (IV-I) cadences.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonic
body: chord I - the 'home' note and chord of a key and the note that the key is named after
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dominant
body: the fifth note in a scale, or the chord based on that note (chord V)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Subdominant
body: chord IV in a key
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Perfect cadence
body: a V-I progression at the end of a section of music; it feels resolved
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: imperfect cadence
body: where part of a chord sequence finishes on the dominant chord (V), which feels unfinished
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Chord IV and V sound the same, so plagal and perfect cadences sound the same.
body: They sound similar, but not identical. Picking out the bass note is the key - if you can hear that note, you can work out how it relates to the tonic, so can work out which chord (and cadence) you are listening to.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers use various common harmonic devices to enhance harmony and create certain musical effects.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Drones, pedals and ground bass are all determined by the bass parts and how they relate to the chords.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Modulations are changes in key that can radically alter the mood of a piece of music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Suspensions are a specific type of dissonance that is used to create harmonic tension and resolution.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pedal
body: a continuous pitch or note in the music which remains the same as the other harmonies change
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: drone
body: a constant, pitched sound that continues throughout a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ground bass
body: a short, repeated bass line that repeats throughout a piece, forming the structure of the music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: modulation
body: a change of key during a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: suspension
body: A mixture of an insoluble solid and liquid in which the solid particles are dispersed in the liquid and settle upon the mixture standing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A modulation is when the chords don't use the tonic.
body: A modulation is actually when the tonic changes. Sometimes music can sound like it will modulate, but then it stays in the same key. For a true modulation, it must feel like the tonic itself has changed.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Time signatures (or metre) can be grouped into simple, compound and irregular time signatures.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Simple time signatures have two quavers in each beat.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Compound time signatures have three quavers in each beat.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Simple and compound time signatures can also be described as duple (2), triple (3) or quadruple (4 beats).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Irregular time signatures cannot be counted with groups of only 2 or only 3 beats. Examples are 7/8 and 5/4.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: simple time
body: each beat is divided into two quavers; 4/4 and 3/4 are examples of this
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Compound time
body: Compound time is when each beat is divided into three quavers, rather than two (e.g. a 12/8 time signature)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: irregular time signature
body: the number of beats cannot be divided by 2 or 3 (e.g. 5, 7)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Compound time signatures create more complex sounding music and aren't used often.
body: This isn't strictly true. Compound time signatures are extremely common, including in popular music styles. While the theory of them is slightly more complex than simple time signatures, to compose or play using them is not particularly difficult.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: There are many different Italian terms to describe tempo, including largo, allegro and presto.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Tempo can also be measured in beats per minute (BPM).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Accelerando, ritardando and rubato change the tempo during a composition.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some of the most common rhythmic features include syncopation, rhythmic motifs and cells and rhythmic repetition.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: rubato
body: a slight speeding up and slowing down of the tempo to show expression
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accelerando
body: when the tempo gradually speeds up
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ritardando
body: a gradual slowing down of tempo; rallentando creates a similar effect
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: swing quavers
body: the first quaver in each pair has a slightly longer duration than the second quaver
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Syncopated
body: a rhythm that emphasises (accents) notes in between the main beats; this is often created by using half-beat rests on the beat or dotted rhythms
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Tempo markings are a precise indication of speed.
body: Most tempo markings (like allegro) are a rough indication of the speed, but not an exact measurement. Composers usually leave it up to the performers to determine the exact speed. Often in modern music they will indicate a specific speed using BPM.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many melodies use an anacrusis to start before beat one (the downbeat).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Polyrhythms include multiple rhythms that aren’t closely related playing together, creating a complex rhythmic texture.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cross rhythms create the feeling of different pulses playing simultaneously.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A hemiola is used to create a brief effect of the pulse changing (by playing three notes over two beats or vice versa).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Diminution and augmentation develop rhythmic ideas by proportionally shortening or lengthening notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: downbeat
body: the first and strongest beat of the bar
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: anacrusis
body: when a melody starts before the downbeat (beat 1)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polyrhythm
body: playing two or more conflicting rhythms at the same time
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cross rhythm
body: a polyrhythm in which two or more of the rhythms 'conflict' and feel like they have a different pulse
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: hemiola
body: when three notes are played over the duration of two or vice versa, creating the feeling of tempo change
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Polyrhythm and cross rhythm are the same thing.
body: They are related, but not the same. A polyrhythm doesn't necessarily have to create different senses of pulse - it can just have different rhythms playing together. A cross rhythm has to create different senses of pulse at the same time.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many styles around the world are defined by idiomatic rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some of these are linked with specific styles, such as skank (reggae), chaal (bhangra) and scotch snap (Celtic folk).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Others have their roots in specific regions, but are used in many styles, such as the clave and tresillo rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some are not specific rhythms, but types of rhythms, such as swing, free rhythms and driving rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: driving rhythms
body: fast, repeated rhythms that create a sense of energy
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: clave
body: a five-note syncopated rhythm with various forms; the most common form is the son clave
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tresillo
body: a three-note rhythm that is the same as the ‘3’ of the son clave
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chaal
body: the name commonly given to a particular distinctive rhythm played on the dhol in bhangra
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: free rhythms
body: when free rhythms are played, they create no clear sense of pulse
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Idiomatic rhythms are rhythms that are only used in a specific style.
body: Idiomatic rhythms are rhythms that are typically associated with that style, but can also be heard in different styles. For example, while the skank rhythm is very idiomatic in reggae, there are many other styles that also repeat off-beat quavers.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Dynamics and articulation have a big impact on musical mood and character.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The most common dynamics are piano (p) and forte (f).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Dynamic changes are indicated with crescendo, diminuendo and subito (sudden) and poco a poco (little by little).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Staccato and legato (slurred) are the most common types of articulation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Different kinds of articulation include accents, tenuto, marcato and sforzando.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: crescendo
body: gradually getting louder
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diminuendo
body: when the dynamics gradually decrease, getting quieter
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accented
body: a note that is emphasised, shown with this symbol: >
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sforzando
body: a sudden, loud type of accent, marked with the abbreviation sfz
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tenuto
body: a note that is held for its full length, though still detached from surrounding notes
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: There is only one type of accent.
body: The regular accent is the most common, but composers often indicate more specific articulation by using other accents such as marcato and sforzando. These can be difficult to distinguish by ear, but as a performer you should be familiar with them.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The orchestra is home to a diverse range of instruments which use different effects to create different timbres.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some common effects include: arco, pizzicato, muted, and double-stopping.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Styles of popular music often use different timbres.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The synthesiser creates a wide range of different sounds, including different synth leads, pads and basses.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: arco
body: when strings are played with a bow
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pizzicato
body: a string technique in which the performer plucks the string with a finger
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: mute
body: a device that dampens and reduces the sound produced by an instrument
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: synth lead
body: a type of synthesised sound that is suited to playing melodies
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: synth pad
body: a type of synthesised sound that is suited to playing sustained sounds
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Instrumental timbres in families can be identified with pitch.
body: This isn't always the case. Instruments such as the trombone and French horn have a similiar pitch and the oboe and cor anglais pitch ranges cross over, so it's important that pupils think about the timbres to identify instruments correctly.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: There is a huge diversity of instruments around the world. Some have crossed between musical genres and traditions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Common non-Western drums include tabla, timbales, conga, djembe and dhol.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: There are many other important percussion instruments, including both tuned and untuned percussion.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: There is also a diverse range of stringed instruments that can be heard.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These include guitar-like instruments like banjo, mandolin and bouzouki, and other instruments like tanpura and sarangi.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tabla
body: a set of two drums on which the taal is played with the hands
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: conga
body: a hand drum originating in Africa with a round, full timbre
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: banjo
body: a guitar-like stringed instrument that has a distinct percussive ‘twangy’ timbre
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sitar
body: a stringed instrument from the Indian subcontinent that creates a rich, ringing timbre with use of its resonant strings
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: It is impossible to memorise the timbre of all of the different instruments around the world.
body: Yes, it would be impossible. However, learning to identify some of the key instruments is valuable - these are often heard in styles across different cultures, so learning the sound of the most common is important as a well-rounded musician.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Vocals are very diverse, with numerous voice types, styles and techniques.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An SATB choir is made up of the following female and male vocal types: soprano, alto, tenor and bass.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some common vocal techniques include melisma, vibrato and rapping.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In some styles, microtonal singing, scat singing and beatboxing can also be heard.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: SATB
body: a type of choir consisting of soprano, alto, tenor and bass singers
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vibrato
body: a vocal or instrumental technique in which the pitch ‘wobbles’ slightly
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melismatic
body: when there are syllables with more than one note sung to them
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: beatboxing
body: a vocal technique that imitates drum kit and percussion sounds
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: falsetto
body: a technique in which male voices can sing much higher than their normal range; it has a distinct, thin, airy timbre
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Female voices are always higher pitched than male voices.
body: While this is mostly true, alto and tenor ranges overlap. A low alto voice can be as low as a tenor. Alongside this, men can use the falsetto technique to sing much higher than their normal range, in some cases higher than female voices.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Technology has hugely influenced the way that music is produced, edited and manipulated.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Synth pads, leads, basses and drum machines are common tools for producing sounds electronically.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Effects can be applied either live or after recording.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some common effects are delay, reverb, chorus, auto-tune, distortion, panning and equalisation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Overdubbing and DJing are two other important ways that technology has shaped modern music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: drum machine
body: an instrument that synthesises drum sounds; the TR-808 is an example
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reverb
body: an effect that creates the impression of a sound being played in a more ‘echoey’ space
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: delay
body: an effect that ‘echoes’ sounds back after a specific time
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: overdubbing
body: adding new recorded sound to a pre-existing recording to create a combined effect
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: scratching
body: a DJing technique where the DJ creates a ‘wika wika’ sound by touching the record
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Music technology consists solely of DAWs and computer-based technology.
body: For modern musicians, computer-based tools such as DAWs are a brilliant way of using technology. However, music technology is much broader than this - synthesisers, amplification, turntables and drum machines are just a few examples.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Texture refers to both the number of different musical lines and the way that they relate to each other.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Common textures include monophonic, homophonic, unison, melody and accompaniment and polyphonic.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Other specific relationships between parts include contrary motion, imitation and harmonisation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: unison
body: performing the same movement at exactly the same time as our partner
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melody and accompaniment
body: a texture consisting of a melody with a clearly separate accompaniment
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polyphonic
body: a texture with more than one equally important melodic line
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: contrary motion
body: where two parts move in opposite directions (e.g. ascending and descending)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: harmonisation
body: when one part plays at the same time as a melody, adding notes that create harmony with the melodic line
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Homophonic and melody and accompaniment textures are the same thing.
body: Melody and accompaniment is a specific type of homophonic texture, often called melody-dominated homophony. This is different to a chordal homophonic texture. To avoid confusion, it is easiest to treat melody and accompaniment as a separate texture.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Basic understanding of the defining features of Baroque, Classical and Romantic music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ability to read treble and bass clef to a basic standard
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Knowledge of different textures, including homophonic, polyphonic, unison, imitative and monophonic.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Understanding of the development of the orchestra through the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Solid grounding in the musical elements with understanding of key terminology for all elements.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Baroque solo concerto features many typical features of Baroque music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These include a typical Baroque orchestra with continuo, and melodic features such as ornamentation and imitation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Baroque concertos create contrast through use of tutti and solo sections, terraced dynamics and contrasting textures.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The three movements of a concerto contrast with each other, and often one or more use ritornello form.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This features a ritornello section that returns throughout.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: concerto
body: a composition for a solo instrument with orchestral accompaniment
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tutti
body: In a tutti passage the whole ensemble plays
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: continuo
body: the accompaniment section of the Baroque orchestra, normally including harpsichord and a bass stringed instrument (e.g. cello)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ritornello
body: a recurring passage in a piece of Baroque music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: terraced dynamics
body: where dynamics change suddenly, rather than gradually
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Melody and accompaniment is not a homophonic texture.
body: There are different kinds of homophonic texture. A chordal homophonic texture is one in which all parts play the same rhythm. Melody and accompaniment is also called melody-dominated homophony, where there is a homophonic texture with a melody above.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The concerto grosso is a type of Baroque concerto that includes more than one soloist.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The group of soloists is called the concertino. It usually has two or three performers, most commonly violin and cello.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The accompanying group is called the ripieno, normally based around strings and continuo.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The concertino and ripieno interact in different ways, creating contrast.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: concerto grosso
body: a type of Baroque concerto that includes more than one soloist
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ripieno
body: the name for the group of accompanying instruments in a concerto grosso
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: concertino
body: the name for the group of soloists in a concerto grosso
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A concerto grosso is exactly the same as a concerto, just with more than one soloist.
body: Because there is more than one soloist, composers can play around with texture and interaction more in a concerto grosso. This means that often there is more variety of interaction between parts in a concerto grosso than a solo concerto.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Classical concerto uses a larger orchestra than Baroque, with no continuo and a broader range of solo instruments.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The first movement typically uses sonata form - exposition, development and recapitulation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The texture is usually melody and accompaniment, with a melody based on balanced phrasing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cadenzas are an opportunity for soloists to show off their technical skill, with virtuosic playing in a free tempo.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cadenza
body: a solo section in a concerto in which the soloist plays in a virtuosic manner
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sonata form
body: a common structure for a piece, based on an exposition, development and recapitulation
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: balanced phrasing
body: where melodic phrases are equal length and complementary melodic shape (also called 'question and answer' form)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melody and accompaniment
body: a texture consisting of a melody with a clearly separate accompaniment
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Cadenzas are always composed.
body: Many cadenzas are composed, but it is common for soloists to improvise (or slightly change) cadenzas to make them more unique and to further show off their own skill.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Romantic concerto mirrored many typical features of Romantic music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These include more complex textures, chromatic harmony, a larger orchestra and an emphasis on intense, expressive music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many Romantic concertos are extremely difficult for soloists and are highly virtuosic.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Bruch’s Violin Concerto reflects many of these typical features.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chromatic
body: a note that is not part of the key or scale
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: virtuosic
body: music that shows off a performer’s technical skill
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: rubato
body: a slight speeding up and slowing down of the tempo to show expression
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cadenza
body: a solo section in a concerto in which the soloist plays in a virtuosic manner
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Romantic music is romantic (i.e. about love).
body: Romantic music is generally expressive and emotional, but is not necessarily linked to the emotion of love. The emotions can be anything from dramatic and terrifying to dark and mournful. The name comes from a broader artistic movement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The piano became a very important instrument in Classical and Romantic concertos.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Its dynamic range, pitch range, expressive abilities and ability to play multiple layers attracted composers to it.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The piano concerto mirrored most of the trends of those periods, though there are some specific ways the piano is used.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These include accompanying orchestral melodies with chords and playing both melody and accompaniment together.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chromatic
body: a note that is not part of the key or scale
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diatonic
body: music which uses only notes that are based in the key (e.g. C major or F minor)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: arpeggio
body: A group of notes from a chord played one after the other, either ascending or descending
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: scalic
body: a melody that uses segments of a scale
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tutti
body: In a tutti passage the whole ensemble plays
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Piano concertos are just the same as other concertos.
body: Not quite. Because of the unique abilities of the piano - including its range and ability to play multiple lines at once - composers use it slightly differently to other instruments. This includes using it to accompany itself, or the orchestra.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know the regular time signatures 3/4, 4/4 and 6/8
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know the constituent parts of folk dance music: melody, chords, bass and percussion
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know that melodies can be modal and that this is a tonality
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Arabic music has a long and complex history and is extremely varied.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Two key instruments in Palestinian folk music are the doumbek and oud.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The doumbek uses three sounds - doum (middle of the drum), tek (edge of the drum) and ka (ring finger on edge of drum).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Palestinian folk music uses a wazn, a rhythmic cycle or pattern. Maqsum and saidi are two examples of this.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: doumbek
body: a drum used in Arabic and Palestinian folk music; it is played with the hands and fingertips
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: oud
body: a stringed instrument with 11 strings used in Arabic and Palestinian music; it is an early predecessor to the guitar
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: wazn
body: a repeating rhythmic cycle or pattern that forms the rhythmic basis of a composition
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: maqsum
body: a common wazn across the Middle East
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: saidi
body: a specific upbeat wazn that uses fast rhythmic patterns
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Hand drum technique is the same across the world.
body: Techniques are very different on different hand drums around the world. Tabla, doumbek and djembe all use very different techniques, for example, the doumbek technique uses fingertips in a way that djembe does not.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Palestinian folk music has many popular forms, many of which are performed for dance.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ataaba is a popular song form in Palestine, and dabke is an important traditional form of dance across the region.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Traditional Palestinian and Arabic music is based on a maqam, which is a set of notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Each maqam is microtonal and includes seven notes. They are usually taught by ear. Bayati is a common maqam.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Performers improvise using the maqam, including in taqsim at the start of a performance.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ataaba
body: a traditional form of solo Palestinian love song that is often heard at weddings and other occasions
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dabke
body: a type of folk dance; it can be performed with different styles of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Microtonal
body: If a melody is microtonal it uses notes in between the 12 notes of the Western scale. It uses intervals smaller than a semitone.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: taqsim
body: an improvised solo based on a maqam that introduces a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: maqam
body: a set of notes, (like a scale) that forms the basis of a composition; it is microtonal and has seven notes
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: There are only 12 possible notes.
body: There is an infinite possible number of notes. Imagine that an octave is a cake. We can divide it into 12 equal slices (12 Western notes) or 24 smaller slices (the Arabic system). In theory, we could divide it into any number of slices/notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Israeli folk music is influenced by various global regions and has strong ties with Jewish folk music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is often used to accompany dance, in particular at celebrations and festive occasions in Israel.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The music is energetic, upbeat and has a strong rhythmic pulse for dancing to.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Its distinct sound comes from its use of off-beat chords, accelerando and ornamentation, including note bends.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Typical instruments include violin, clarinet and accordion.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accelerando
body: when the tempo gradually speeds up
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: note bending
body: when a musician ‘bends’ the pitch of a note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ornamentation
body: when a performer decorates a melody with extra notes (e.g. trills, turns)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Israeli music is very similar to other Middle Eastern music because Israel is in the Middle East.
body: Israeli folk music has a very different history to other music from the region, as it was influenced by Jewish migrants from other parts of the world. Jewish folk music uses many European instruments and has similarities with European folk music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Greek folk music includes both folk songs and music for dance.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It uses a mix of common Western instruments and traditional Greek instruments, including the bouzouki and defi.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Much Greek folk music uses irregular time signatures such as 5/8 and 7/8.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Kalamatianó is a type of Greek folk dance which is based in 7/8.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Usually 7/8 is counted as a 3-2-2. 5/8 is counted as 3-2.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bouzouki
body: a traditional Greek stringed instrument
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: defi
body: a type of tambourine, a small hand drum with bangles
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: irregular time signature
body: the number of beats cannot be divided by 2 or 3 (e.g. 5, 7)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: kalamatianó
body: a type of Greek folk dance which is based in 7/8 metre
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Music for dance must have a regular pulse (in 2, 3 or 4).
body: While most Western dance music has a regular time signature, in other parts of the world it is common to dance to music with irregular time signatures, such as 5/8 and 7/8.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The bouzouki has a characteristic playing style that uses slides and tremolo.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Instrumental and vocal melodies are often harmonised with thirds.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Melodies in Greek folk music are mostly conjunct and use ornamentation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The vocal melodies are often conjunct and melismatic, like in Thalassaki Mou.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: third
body: an interval of three notes. When both notes are performed together, the harmony would be described as ‘3rds’
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: slide
body: To observe a specimen using a light microscope, we have to put a thin layer of it on a glass microscope slide.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tremolo
body: alternating between two notes rapidly; sounds like a trembling effect
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melismatic
body: when there are syllables with more than one note sung to them
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Conjunct
body: movement between notes based on small intervals (steps)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The bouzouki sounds the same as a guitar.
body: The bouzouki has very specific techniques that give it its characteristic sound. These include use of tremolo, slides and thirds. Although these can be used on the guitar, they are not as common as on the bouzouki.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have been introduced to a range of different musical starting points for composition including melodic ideas, chords and bass lines
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have composed short melodies, motifs and riffs and triad chord progressions
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have developed short compositional ideas within recommended genres
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils can interpret notation and follow a score
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have extended chord sequences by using inversions and broken chords
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have been introduced to dissonance
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Good melodies use some repetition and have a distinctive shape and can use conjunct and disjunct intervals.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Melodies all have rhythm. There are a variety of rhythmic choices that can be used to reflect the character of a melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A melody can be expressive with appropriate tempo, dynamics and articulation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: disjunct
body: movement between notes that involves intervals larger than two semitones (moving by leap)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Conjunct
body: movement between notes based on small intervals (steps)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: interval
body: the distance in pitch between two notes (e.g. a fifth)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: articulation
body: Articulation is how the note is played eg. legato, staccato or accented.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Using disjunct intervals in a melody means the notes can be placed anywhere.
body: Disjunct intervals need a sense of order to the music and should be used in some sort of pattern in the same way that conjunct intervals should.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers often create chord progressions to underpin their music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: You can start with a chord progression before you create a melody, or start with a melody then add chords.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adding chords to a melody is called harmonisation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: You can create dissonance by using chords that are not triads and using occasional melody notes from outside the chord.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Broken chords and chord inversions can add interest to a chord progression.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Chord progression
body: A chord progression (or chord sequence) is a repeating pattern of chords.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: harmonisation
body: when one part plays at the same time as a melody, adding notes that create harmony with the melodic line
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Triad
body: A triad is a chord made up of three notes from the scale: the root, third and fifth.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dissonance
body: where notes in a chord clash, creating harmonic tension
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: inversion
body: when the subject pronoun and the verb switch place to form a question
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Harmony and chords are the same thing.
body: Although the harmony is created by the different notes of the chord progression, harmony also includes all parts in the music including the melodic line.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The rhythm and syllables of words can help us create rhythmic variety in our compositions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Variety is important as it creates interest for the listener, so we need to use both simple and complex rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can also use syncopation and polyrhythms to create interest.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using repeated patterns or an ostinato allows the music to have a sense of unity.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ostinato
body: a short, repeating musical idea (plural: ostinati)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polyrhythm
body: playing two or more conflicting rhythms at the same time
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: syncopation
body: a rhythm which emphasises (accents) notes in between the main beats, often referred to as off-beat rhythms
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: To compose a rhythm we need to consider notation first.
body: It is important to encourage pupils not to be restricted by only rhythms they can notate and for them to experiment with rhythmic patterns that they like musically. Highlight that individual note durations such as a crotchet are not rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Texture is an important element to consider when composing. Melody and accompaniment is the most common musical texture.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers also use homophonic, polyphonic and monophonic textures.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In a melody and accompaniment texture the lead line or melody should be clear.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Less important musical lines can contrast by using less interesting rhythms and melodic shapes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: monophonic
body: a texture that consists of a single line of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: melody and accompaniment
body: a texture consisting of a melody with a clearly separate accompaniment
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polyphonic
body: a texture with more than one equally important melodic line
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A piece of music has a fixed texture all the way through
body: Although we can describe some pieces of music as particular textures overall there are often sections within pieces where the texture changes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When writing for instruments music has to be playable and maximise the unique characteristics of the instrument.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Range, intervals and how the instrument can be played is important in idiomatic writing for an instrument.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some instruments can change timbre i.e. strings can play bowed or pizzicato.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Timbre can also be changed for expressive purposes, including using vibrato.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Creative use of timbre can add interest and variety to compositions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: timbre
body: the description of the sound or tone of an instrument
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: idiomatic writing
body: Idiomatic writing is composing for an instrument (acoustic or electronic) or voice that makes the best use of the distinctive properties of that instrument or voice.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vibrato
body: a vocal or instrumental technique in which the pitch ‘wobbles’ slightly
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: An instrument only has one timbre.
body: An instrument can have a few different timbres. Give examples of how instruments can change the sound they make.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils recognise the sound of blues and rock'n'roll
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have the fluency to play chords and bass lines into a DAW
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know how to use a DAW to record vocals
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils have experience improvising on a pentatonic scale
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Rock 'n' roll is an energetic style that developed in the 1950s.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It was very popular with young people and became the first successful pop style.

title: Blues is an old style of music that isn't relevant anymore.
body: While it's true that blues first developed more than a century ago, it continued to be an important style all through the 20th century and up to the present day. It shaped many different styles (including rock) that came to be incredibly important.

body: Rock 'n' roll is an energetic style that developed in the 1950s from blues and country music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It incorporates key blues features including the 12-bar blues, walking bass and swing/shuffle rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Driving rhythms and intense 'shouty' vocals help to give rock 'n' roll its distinctive style.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Other key features include a fast tempo, vocal melodies with a small range of notes and a verse-chorus structure.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Typical instrumentation includes vocals, electric guitar, piano, drum kit and bass guitar or double bass.

title: Unison and homophonic textures are the same thing and unison parts have to be played in the same octave.
body: In a unison texture, both the pitch and rhythm of the part must be the same. In a homophonic texture, only the rhythm needs to be the same - the parts can play different notes or chords. Parts played in octaves are also classed as a unison texture.

title: If the bass stays on the same note, this is a pedal.
body: This is not quite true. It is only a pedal if the bass note stays the same while the chords change above it. If the chords do not change, it cannot be a pedal.

body: Bhangra is a traditional Punjabi dance and form of music that has its roots in farming communities of the Punjab.

body: Chaal is a rhythm in 4/4, with each beat divided in three. It emphasises beat one and four.

body: Typically chaal is played on a two-headed drum called a dhol, or sometimes a smaller version called a dholak.

title: Bhangra is a style of music from South Asia.
