body: the process of creating and using a sample
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Synthesizer
body: A synthesizer is an electronic instrument that can create a wide variety of different timbres.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chord sequence
body: a pattern of chords that usually lasts for 4, 8 or 16 bars
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Bhangra is a traditional style of music that doesn't use music technology extensively.
body: Modern bhangra uses many of the tools that are available to musicians now, including different applications of music technology. It uses these to enhance the music, while still having its roots embedded in the traditional features of Punjabi bhangra.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The music of Latin America is extremely varied.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many styles are influenced by colonial history, drawing on European, Asian, African and indigenous American music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many styles use Latin percussion instruments, including woodblock, claves, guiro, congas, bongos and maracas.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: There are often complex syncopated rhythms, including the son clave and rumba clave rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A clave rhythm can be arranged as a 3-2 clave or a 2-3 clave.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Latin America
body: Spanish and Portugese-speaking parts of Central and South America are referred to as Latin America.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Latin percussion
body: Latin percussion instruments are those that are common in Latin American music. Examples include cabasa, guiro, claves and maracas.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Syncopated
body: a rhythm that emphasises (accents) notes in between the main beats; this is often created by using half-beat rests on the beat or dotted rhythms
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Son clave
body: The Cuban son clave is the most common clave rhythm.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Rumba clave
body: The rumba clave is another common clave rhythm, with the last note of the ‘3’ delayed by a quaver.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The 2:3 clave starts on the same beat as the 3:2 clave.
body: The 2:3 clave starts with a crotchet rest. Make sure when performing or recording this that you count 'rest, 1, 2' for the '2' section of the rhythm.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Salsa and merengue are popular forms of music and dance that both use Latin percussion and syncopated rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Key features of salsa include the piano montuno, tresillo bass pattern and son clave rhythm.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Salsa often uses a large band, similar to a Western jazz ‘big band’ with saxophones, brass, and a rhythm section.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Merengue typically has a smaller group, using traditional Dominican instruments such as the tambora.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The quintillo is a defining rhythmic pattern in merengue.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Salsa
body: Salsa is a style of music and dance that developed from Cuban son music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Montuno
body: A montuno is a syncopated, repeating piano pattern that is typical of salsa.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tresillo
body: a three-note rhythm that is the same as the ‘3’ of the son clave
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Merengue
body: Merengue is a style of music and dance from the Dominican Republic that often uses traditional Dominican instruments.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Quintillo
body: A quintillo is a rhythmic pattern of five fast notes that is a typical feature of merengue.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Latin dance music all sounds the same.
body: Many of the styles of music from this region include similar features, such as syncopated rhythms, Latin percussion, Spanish lyrics etc. However, they all have distinct differences that allow us to tell the different traditions apart.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Calypso and mento are important musical styles from the Caribbean that have their roots in colonial history.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: While they have some similar features, there are big differences in lyrics, origins and instrumentation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Soca is a repetitive, catchy upbeat style that developed from calypso in the 1970s as a form of dance music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: All three styles use some similar syncopated rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Steel pans are a key part of the culture of Trinidad and Tobago, and often perform calypso as well as other styles.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: calypso
body: a style of music from Trinidad and Tobago where lyrics are often improvised and often on a topical theme
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Mento
body: Mento is a Jamaican style of music with many similarities to calypso.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Soca
body: Soca (short for ‘soul of Calypso’) is an upbeat style that developed out of Calypso in the 1970s. It is often heard at carnival and used for dancing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Steel pans
body: Steel pans are pitched percussion instruments from Trinidad and Tobago. They come in different sizes/pitches and are often used in large bands.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Calypso, mento and soca are different versions of the same musical style.
body: Although they have superficial similarities, these are all distinct styles with different features and histories. Soca is strongly linked to calypso and can be seen as an offshoot of that style, but mento is a completely separate tradition.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Samba is a form of Brazilian dance and music which comes in many forms, one of which is batucada.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Batucada is often played at celebrations and carnival, and is performed by a percussion ensemble called a bateria.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Bossa nova adapts many of the features of samba to create a more relaxed style.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It often uses a version of the clave called the bossa nova clave.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many other styles exist in the region, including habanera, tango, danzón, cha-cha-chá and rumba.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: samba
body: Samba is a style of energetic Brazilian dance, or the music that goes with it.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: batucada
body: Batucada is a type of fast-paced samba music performed by a percussion ensemble (bateria).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bossa nova
body: Bossa nova is a style of music and dance that developed from samba in the 1950s.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bossa nova clave
body: The bossa nova clave is a version of the clave in which the second note of the ‘2’ is delayed by a quaver.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: habanera
body: a two beat rhythm that uses dotted notes and an accented upbeat
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may confuse the bossa nova clave and rumba clave with each other.
body: Break the bossa nova clave into its group of 3 and group of 2. Practise the '3' on its own, identically to the son clave. Then practise the '2' with the second note delayed by a quaver. Only once the two parts are separately learnt then combine them.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Reggae grew out of ska and rocksteady to become an important style of music in Jamaica and around the world.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Reggae often expresses political messages and addresses social issues.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some of its defining characteristics are the skank rhythm on electric guitar, one-drop drum beat and reggae bubble.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Those features all emphasise the offbeats, and avoid emphasising the usual strong beats (one and three).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The bass line often plays on the strong beats, sticking out from the other rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ska
body: Ska is an upbeat style of music that emerged in the late 1960s in Jamaica. It later developed into a style called rocksteady.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reggae
body: Reggae is a style that emergend in the late 1960s and became an important global style.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: skank
body: The skank rhythm is a defining feature of reggae that emphasises offbeat quavers.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reggae bubble
body: The reggae bubble is a typical organ pattern that emphasises offbeats.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: one-drop
body: The one-drop beat is a typical reggae drum beat, which removes the usual emphasis on beat one.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Drum beats should emphasise the start of each bar.
body: Most pop and rock drum beats do this, but many other musical styles do not emphasise beat one. The one-drop beat starts with a rest on beat one, and emphasises beat two and four.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know that tonality can be major, minor or modal
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know how to recognise the use of sequence in a melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know how to play a melody on the keyboard from reading the treble clef
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know how to use a scale to improvise new material in a DAW that is then notated
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Harmony and tonality have a significant impact on the mood of film music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers use atonal, diatonic (major or minor) or modal tonality to create different moods.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The choice of chords and use of chromatic harmony are also important for creating the correct emotions for the scene.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Reharmonising a melody, by changing the harmony, is an effective way to develop a melodic idea in a film.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonality
body: the type of notes and chords that a piece of music is based on (e.g. minor, major, atonal)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diatonic
body: music which uses only notes that are based in the key (e.g. C major or F minor)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chromatic
body: a note that is not part of the key or scale
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: modal
body: music based on a mode, a type of scale different from major and minor scales
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reharmonisation
body: when a composer keeps a melody the same but changes the harmony
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Chromatic and atonal are the same thing.
body: Atonal music sounds chromatic, because there is no clear tonal centre. However, chromatic music isn't necessarily atonal - a piece can be in a key, but use chromatic notes from outside of it.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Harmonic devices, such as pedals and dissonance are very useful tools for film composers.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pedals (usually on the tonic note) create tension by creating clashes between the bass notes and chords.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Dissonant chords, which often feature adjacent notes or chromatic notes, also create tension and excitement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can reharmonise a consonant melody with dissonant harmony to develop it and add tension.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pedal
body: a continuous pitch or note in the music which remains the same as the other harmonies change
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonic
body: chord I - the 'home' note and chord of a key and the note that the key is named after
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dissonance
body: where notes in a chord clash, creating harmonic tension
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: consonance
body: where notes in a chord sound pleasant together, without tension
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Black notes are the same thing as chromatic notes.
body: This is not always true. Chromatic notes are any notes that are from outside of the key. If you are in C major, which only uses white notes, the black notes will be chromatic. However, in other keys the black notes might not be chromatic.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Rhythm and texture are crucial elements to develop when creating music for action scenes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Repeating ostinati, driving rhythms and accents can create a sense of energy and excitement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Thickening the texture also builds energy and excitement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using these strategies, a simple melodic idea can be developed into exciting music for an action scene.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Driving rhythm
body: A driving rhythm is one that repeats fast notes to create a sense of energy.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ostinato
body: a short, repeating musical idea (plural: ostinati)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accent
body: an emphasis on a note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: texture
body: how something feels when it is touched
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: doubling
body: Doubling is the act of becoming twice as many.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Repetitive film music is not very interesting and can't build excitement.
body: Music that repeats ideas can build excitement if the composer develops aspects of it. By adding layers, changing rhythms and developing the texture, a simple repeated idea can be developed into an exciting musical soundworld.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Writing film music requires composers to precisely match their music to the timings of action.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They use storyboards to represent the action of a scene and cues to help fit their music to exact moments in a scene.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They create the music to match each mood, by developing musical ideas in different ways.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Developing an ostinato to create different moods.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ostinato
body: a short, repeating musical idea (plural: ostinati)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: development
body: improving and building on design ideas to make them better
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: All film music has to be precise to the second to fit the action perfectly.
body: Some film scenes do have to be exact where the music mirrors precisely what is happening on screen, but much film music is about creating the correct atmosphere and feel and this can be just as important when composing programmatic music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Film composers have to carefully match musical changes to precise cues and timestamps.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Manipulating the tempo is one method that helps to fit sections of music to specific timings.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Sometimes transitions between sections are deliberately sudden to match sudden changes in the action.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers can also make more musical transitions by ‘blending’ features of the two sections to create a seamless change.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cue
body: a signal to a performer
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: timestamp
body: a specific moment in time in a composition (e.g. 01:25 - 1 minute and 25 seconds)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: musical transition
body: when two sections of music are linked in a coherent and musically satisfying way
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Changes between moods in a scene should always be sudden.
body: This is not always the case. Sometimes it is more appropriate to create a gradual change so that the shift isn't dramatically obvious. This might be where there is a gradual change of mood or action in a scene.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers develop their musical ideas by exploring different ways of transforming the material.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Sequence, retrograde and inversion are compositional devices that we can use to transform melodic ideas.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A balance of repetition and contrast is important in making your music interesting but memorable.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: New ideas can be derived from already established ones by developing a few interesting, distinctive ideas.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sequence
body: a short melodic idea that is repeated in steps either rising or falling
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: retrograde
body: when a set of notes (like a tone row) is reversed
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: inversion
body: when the subject pronoun and the verb switch place to form a question
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Sequence, retrograde and inversion are they only way to develop ideas and they have to be used perfectly.
body: Sequences, retrograde and inversion provide a concrete way for pupils to show development in their melodic ideas, but providing there is some similarity or recognisable quality in repeated ideas, any subtle changes within melodic ideas can work.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Changing the harmonic rhythm can add interest to a composition. It can dramatically alter the mood in a piece.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Harmonic devices such as pedal notes and drones are useful for building harmonic tension and adding colour.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By adding extensions to chords, composers can enhance the expressive qualities of chord sequences.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Harmonic rhythm
body: Harmonic rhythm is how often the chords change.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pedal note
body: A pedal note is a bass note that stays the same while chords change above it.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: drone
body: a constant, pitched sound that continues throughout a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: extended chord
body: an extended chord is a chord that includes more than three different notes
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A pedal note is just a long, low note.
body: A pedal note is a consistent pitch usually in the bass whilst the chords change. Encourage pupils to listen to and experiment with the pitch they choose for a pedal to hear the effect it has on the harmony.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers should carefully consider how to use rhythm.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers can use augmentation and diminution to develop musical ideas, such as new melodic ideas or countermelodies.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Our composing skills develop through making the most of small musical ideas.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using rhythmic devices creates interest and variety for the listener.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Augmentation
body: the process of lengthening all of the notes in a melody by the same proportion
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Diminution
body: the process of shortening all of the notes in a melody by the same proportion
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: countermelody
body: a second melody that plays at the same time as the main melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Augmentation and diminution are not the same as augmented and diminished.
body: Augmentation and diminution are devices that affect the rhythm of music. Augmented and diminished are types of chords and refer to the harmony of music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To create contrast in a composition it is important to vary the texture and timbre.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This might include changing which part plays the melody and which parts are accompanying.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers use a range of accompaniment patterns to create the mood and character in the music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These include broken chords and Alberti bass patterns.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They change these patterns to create variety and contrast between sections.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accompaniment
body: a part in the music that supports the melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: broken chord
body: when the notes of a chord are sounded one at a time
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Alberti bass
body: A group of notes rom a chord played in a specific pattern of lowest note, highest note, middle note, highest note
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Broken chords have to be in the triad position where the root is the lowest note.
body: Broken chords like block chords can be played in different inversions and this can make them more interesting.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When musical material returns, composers often make subtle changes to it.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Keeping the melody and harmony recognisable is important when developing repeated sections.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In new sections, like a B section in ternary form, new melodic and harmonic ideas can be derived from earlier sections.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This maintains the coherence of the music and shows understanding of how musical elements can be explored creatively.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Ternary form
body: Ternary form is a musical structure in three sections, with the first section repeated at the end. It is also referred to as ABA.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Melodic material
body: Melodic material refers to musical ideas that contribute to the melody (e.g. the melody and key musical ideas such as motifs, riffs or counter melodies).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Harmonic material
body: Harmonic material refers to musical ideas that contribute to harmony of the music (e.g. the chords and chord sequence, the bass line and devices, including pedals).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Contrasting sections should be totally different to other sections in a composition.
body: Contrasting sections of music can be derived from some of the same ideas but should have their own recognisable melodic and harmonic ideas.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: North Indian classical music typically involves three features - rhythm, melody and drone.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The sitar typically plays the melody, accompanied by rhythms on the tabla and a sustained drone on the tanpura.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: North Indian classical music is based on raga. Each raga is a set of notes that has a specific mood associated with it.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Performers improvise using a raga to create the alap section.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This is the first section in a piece of North Indian classical music, in which there is no clear pulse.

body: Singing in North Indian classical music can be in many languages, most commonly Hindi and Urdu.

title: Microtonal

title: Teental is in 4/4.
body: Teental sounds to us like it could be in 4/4, but this is just a coincidence. North Indian classical musicians don't think of time signature in the same way that we do - the tala is what structures the time and they can be many different lengths.

body: North Indian classical music has a typical structure consisting of alap, gat and jhala.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alap is the introduction, with a free tempo and the sitar player improvising on the raga.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In gat, there is a clear pulse on the tabla, and a more structured melody on the sitar.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In jhala, it speeds up and the performers play more complex music in a virtuosic style, building to a frantic finale.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Alap
body: The introduction section to a piece of North Indian classical music is called alap.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Gat
body: The second section, where the tabla joins in is called gat. It has a more fixed melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Jhala
body: The final section, where the tempo and energy builds, is called jhala.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: virtuosic
body: music that shows off a performer’s technical skill
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The alap - gat - jhala structure is just about changes in tempo from slow, to medium to fast.
body: While the tempo does change, the bigger changes are around melody. The alap explores the raga freely, the gat is more structured and the jhala is heavily improvised and virtuosic.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: West Africa has a long history of music and dance. Many Western styles can trace their roots back to this region.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: While the music is extremely varied, many traditional styles have similar features and instrumentation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Most traditional styles in the region use percussion instruments, including djembe, agogo bell, dunun and shekere.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Polyrhythm and cross rhythms are common features across various traditions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Most of these traditions combine music and dance together.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: djembe
body: a goblet-shaped hand drum originating in West Africa
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Agogo bell
body: An agogo bell is a metal instrument consisting of two pitched bells. It is played with a stick.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Dunun
body: A dunun is a large two-headed drum played with a stick. Often a bell is also attached.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polyrhythm
body: playing two or more conflicting rhythms at the same time
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cross rhythm
body: a polyrhythm in which two or more of the rhythms 'conflict' and feel like they have a different pulse
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A cross rhythm is when two players play in different time signatures.
body: A cross rhythm only sounds like there are different time signatures at the same time, but in reality they both use the same time signature (but sound otherwise).

body: West African percussive music is often rhythmically complex.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: West African musicians traditionally don't use notation, but instead learn rhythms by ear and through movement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A compound time signature has each beat divided into three quavers. 6/8 is a common example of this.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In a simple time signature each beat is divided into two quavers.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some West African music has a feel of compound time, including akom and dununba.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: simple time
body: each beat is divided into two quavers; 4/4 and 3/4 are examples of this
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Compound time
body: Compound time is when each beat is divided into three quavers, rather than two (e.g. a 12/8 time signature)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polyrhythm
body: playing two or more conflicting rhythms at the same time
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Dununba
body: Dununba is a type of dance and music in compound time from Guinea.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Dance music is usually in 4/4.
body: While the majority of modern Western dance music is in 4/4, dance music around the world (and throughout history) often uses different time signatures, including 3/.4, 6/8 and 12/8, as well as others.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Accurate description of a melody should include its shape and intervals as well as any melodic devices.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A description of tonality should identify whether the music is diatonic (major or minor), modal, atonal or microtonal.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Harmony encompasses the types of chords used, harmonic rhythm, cadences and harmonic devices.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A description of texture should describe the specific texture (e.g. homophonic) and any changes that occur.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: scalic

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: specific techniques used in melodies, including ornamentation and sequences
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tonality

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: composition techniques that affect the harmony, including pedals and modulations
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Harmony and tonality are the same thing.
body: Tonality is to the type of notes and chords that are used (e.g. major). Harmony is the way the notes and chords are used within that key. Think of tonality as a language (e.g. English) and harmony as the word choice and order in a sentence.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A description of rhythm should mention specific note lengths or patterns, as well as any idiomatic rhythms.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A description of metre and tempo should use technical terms (e.g. presto) and identify tempo changes (e.g. rubato).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Timbre encompasses both the instruments that are used and the specific sounds or techniques used on them (e.g. muted).
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Describing articulation and dynamics refers to how the note is played and how loud or soft the music is.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Metre
body: A metre is a standardised unit of measurement. We can abbreviate metre to m.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: timbre
body: the description of the sound or tone of an instrument
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: articulation
body: Articulation is how the note is played eg. legato, staccato or accented.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A description of timbre should only describe the sound qualities heard.
body: While this should be included, it is also important to remember to describe the instruments that have been used, and if they from a particular ensemble. Remember that one instrument can also create multiple timbres.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The main thing I need to remember for long-form answers is the elements acronym (e.g. MAD T SHIRTT).
body: These acronyms do help us to remember what the elements are, but it is much more important in these longer descriptions to ensure answers are clearly structured, thorough and concise, and that correct technical vocabulary is used for each element.

body: Most composers have a purpose in mind when they write music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This might be to tell a story (e.g. programme music), create a mood or encourage dancing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers use the musical elements in specific ways to suit the purpose of their music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can create a sophisticated description of music if we link the elements to the purpose of the music.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: First we describe the element, then describe its effect, then analyse how that fits the purpose.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Musical element

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: When describing music, just describing each element is enough.
body: For some questions, it may be appropriate just to describe each element. However, often we should give a more sophisticated response that links each element to the compositional purpose - why did the composer use that and why is it suitable?
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The way we structure a description is dependent on the question.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: If the question is linked to a particular style or context, every point must link to that.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: If the question is linked to a musical purpose (e.g. depicting a specific scene) every point should link to that.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: If it is a comparison, every feature that is described should be compared to the other clip.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Being concise, making only relevant points and using technical vocabulary are also key to effective responses.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Choosing elements to discuss is just a case of thinking of the easiest ones to talk about.

body: Video game music has transformed as computer technology has developed over the last 50 years.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Modern video game music fulfils similar roles to film music - creating mood, energy and helping to ‘tell the story’.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Video game music is based on repeating linear loops that need to be able to repeat indefinitely.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is also adaptive, changing in response to the player’s actions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Video game theme songs should capture the overall mood and atmosphere of the game.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: theme song
body: a piece of music that introduces a film or game and captures its overall atmosphere
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: linear loop
body: a repeating musical idea in a video game that can be looped indefinitely
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: adaptive music
body: music that can change by reacting to a stimulus; video game music reacts to the player's actions
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Video games composers just have to compose different music for different scenes, like a film composer.
body: To be really effective, it is more complex than this. The music they compose must be able to repeat indefinitely, while sounding musically interesting. It also has to seamlessly transition into different moods, reacting to changes in the action.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is important that a video game theme song captures the atmosphere of the game.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For a high-energy racing game, the theme song should create a feeling of excitement and energy.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can use fast, rhythmic percussion layers to add excitement.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We can also create an energetic driving bass line to add to this energy, including using chord notes and passing notes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a piece of music that introduces a film or game and captures its overall atmosphere
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chord tone
body: a note that is included within a chord
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: passing note
body: a melodic note not from the chord, linking two chord tones
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Complex music sounds most exciting and energetic.
body: Not necessarily - sometimes the most energetic music is that which emphasises the pulse and uses driving rhythms. Sometimes if music is too complex, with many busy layers of sound, it can sound chaotic and messy rather than energetic.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Video game composers make music adaptive by using linear loops and vertical layering.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This allows music to quickly and seamlessly respond to changes caused by a player’s actions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adding (or removing) layers to develop the texture is one way to do vertical layering.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adding a harmonised melody is another common tool used by composers for this purpose.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Reharmonising a melody is as simple as playing it a third higher.
body: While this can be effective, for certain melodies this won't work effectively. Instead, experimenting with the harmonised melody both above and below the main melody is key, as well as experimenting with 3rds and 6ths.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adaptive music in video games uses two techniques to respond to a player’s actions.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These are vertical layering and horizontal resequencing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In horizontal resequencing, new sections of contrasting music are used to match big changes in the game.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many different sections are created, so that the music can respond to any one of the possible changes.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A typical example is using different musical ideas to represent victory or loss in a racing game.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: horizontal resequencing
body: where a new section of music begins in response to a player's action
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vertical layering
body: where layers of music are 'stacked' on top of each other and change in response to the player’s actions
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: In horizontal resequencing, new musical sections should completely contrast with the preceeding section.
body: There should be contrast, but there also needs to be a feeling of continuity. Using some consistent features (like tempo, key, timbre) can help to create a feeling of some continuity, while still creating a large contrast.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Video game composers must check that transitions between sections work musically, in all possible sequences.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Dovetailing of melodies is an effective way of linking sections.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Key changes, in particular, can sound unnatural and jarring.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When analysing unfamiliar music, we can analyse the use of vertical layering and horizontal resequencing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Identifying the type of loops used and the mood created can suggest what type and era of video game it is.

title: Sudden tempo changes do not work in horizontal resequencing.
body: Sometimes tempo changes can sound jarring and unnatural, but sometimes video game composers want to create a sudden change of pace. If done carefully, tempo changes can work effectively.

title: Using chords from within a minor key creates a dark mood.
body: It's more complex than that - it is important to carefully choose which chords within the key you emphasise to create a dark mood. Emphasising chord i and other minor chords helps to make it feel dark and ominous, rather than any chords from the key.

title: The genre of the music tells us exactly what kind of film it is.
body: This is not always true. Sometimes composers deliberately use genres that go against expectations. This might be for humour, or to create a strange clash. A good example would be A Knight's Tale, which uses modern genres in a medieval film.

body: Leitmotif is a technique that developed from opera and programme music in the 19th century.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Leitmotifs are used to represent characters, places or ideas.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They often change to match changes in the story.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We must carefully consider the musical elements to make sure that the leitmotif suits the character or idea.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This includes harmony, tonality (major and minor), rhythm, timbre, articulation and dynamics.

title: A leimotif is just a musical theme.
body: Not quite. A leitmotif is a musical idea that must represent something else. This is usually a character, place or idea. A musical theme can exist without representing anything at all.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Leitmotifs must reflect the character or mood of what they represent.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Carefully planning how to use the musical elements such as tonality and rhythm is a key part of this.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: However, we must also consider how melodic shape affects the character of a leitmotif.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using conjunct or disjunct intervals in a melody can also shape the mood or feeling that it creates.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: One feature on its own will make a leitmotif have a particular mood.
body: The mood of a leitmotif comes from a combination of different musical elements, including melodic features. Changing one feature might slightly change the mood, but to create a strong mood you need to consider all different aspects of the leitmotif.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Developing a leitmotif to reflect changes in the story is called motivic transformation.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Composers do this in many different ways, including extending or combining leitmotifs.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Reharmonising leitmotifs by changing the harmony but keeping the melody the same is an effective technique.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Changing features of the leitmotif such as rhythm, dynamics, articulation and tonality is also common.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Key to motivic transformation is keeping the leitmotif recognisable and matching the mood of the moment in the story.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: To create a contrasting version of a leitmotif, you should change lots of features of it.
body: You must be careful to not change it too much. If you do, it becomes unrecognisable and will just sound like a different leitmotif. A leitmotif represents a character, place, or idea, so we need to be able to recognise it to link it to that thing.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Chord inversions are inserted randomly by composers.
body: Chord inversions are used to add interest by bringing subtle amounts of tension to a chord and to create smoother transitions from one chord to another. They are not chosen randomly and are used sparingly to create a particular effect.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Changing the voicing of a chord is the same as changing the chord inversion.
body: They are not the same thing. The inversion of the chord is determined by which note is at the bottom (the root or a different note). The voicing is how the notes are spread above this - whether they are close together or far apart.

title: Phrase structure
body: The phrase structure is the pattern of phrases in a melody. It should have a balance of repetition and contrast.

title: Writing a vocal melody is the same as writing an instrumental melody.
body: Many of the same principles apply, such as phrase structure and using notes from the chords and the key. However, a vocal melody has to fit the natural rhythms and mood of the words well - we don't have to consider this with instrumental melodies.

title: The main difference between the verse and chorus is the lyrics.
body: Although that is an important difference, the verse and chorus usually have contrasting moods. This is achieved by creating contrasting chord sequences, textures, rhythms and melodies, not just using different lyrics.

body: Pop ballads typically build to an emotional climax in the final chorus.

body: A typical modulation for a pop ballad is to modulate up a tone (two semitones).

title: To create a good countermelody, you just need two melodies playing at the same time.
body: It's a bit more complicated than that. An effective countermelody has to contrast with the main melody, so that it can be heard. This is done by choosing an appropriate timbre and octave, and using the 'space' in the main melody.

body: Move: effective sprinting technique requires appropriate stride length, high knees and strong elbow drive.

body: the second phase of the race in the first 20m following the start

title: At the beginning of a sprint performance, pupils will rise up into an upright position as soon as possible.
body: An effective drive phase of sprinting sees the body gradually rise up over the first 20m before assuming an upright position. Trying to get upright too soon after starting will hinder acceleration.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: use a sprint start to power yourself into the drive phase and accelerate quickly towards your maximal speed.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: during the drive phase use effective technique to move with maximal possible speed.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: understanding which phase the race is in and adapting technique to the phase will maximise your performance.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: being determined, even during the final phase when fatigued, will help to achieve the best possible time.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: congratulate all your opponents at the end of the race to demonstrate mutual respect.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils will tire during the latter phases of a 100m sprint race and may withdraw their effort because fatigue is setting in and they expected to perform at maximal throughout.
body: Fatigue will always feature in the final stages if the athlete is giving it their best. Recognising this by remaining determined to finish and maintaining technique will result in the best possible time.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: maintaining an effective smooth, upright and relaxed running technique will maximise the use of energy.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: discovering a pace which is sustainable for you and performing it consistently will aid performance in races.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: making good decisions about the pace you can sustain will positively impact your personal best.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: self-assessing your condition during performance will help to select and apply the optimal pace going forward.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may perform middle distances by jogging the majority to conserve energy and putting a sprint in at the end. This often leads to pupils wishing they had put more effort into the initial stages.
body: A well performed 800m requires a fine line between holding back some energy for the finish but also performing at around 80-90% maximum effort for around the first 600m.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: running at a pace which is suited to your personal capabilities will help manage your energy and kick finish.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: ‘kicking’ at an ideal moment towards the end of the race will improve finish time and overtake opponents.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: constantly assess your condition and position to decide whether and when to kick.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: remaining confident and focused on your pacing strategy will ensure you perform at your maximal level.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: encouraging others when they are taking part in their races can motivate them to perform at their best.

title: Pupils expend far too much energy by sprint starting instead of finding their race pace, leading them to tire in the second half of the race.
body: Pupils should focus on finding their race pace, not getting over excited at the start line, beginning too fast or being influenced by others who do. Ideally, the second half of the race is completed quicker than the first (called a negative split).
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: a measured approach with the dominant foot hitting the board at the ideal point will allow for a maximal distance.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: performing a flight phase which allows the body to hang and prepare for landing increases the distance jumped.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: taking off at a 20 degree angle will ensure the optimal transfer of momentum.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: by preparing mentally before the approach, you can perform with maximal effort showing self-motivation.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: supporting the accurate measurement of each other's approach distance will ensure best results can be achieved.

title: Pupils believe starting their approach from the furthest point on the runway will result in the best possible approach and jump.
body: The approach is personalised and should be measured to ensure optimal speed is reached and the take off is smooth without the need to break stride. For most, the end of the runway will not be the ideal starting point.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: an effective combination of approach, hop, step and jump combine to perform a maximal and legal jump.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: an effective triple jump requires each stage of hop, step and jump to cover approximately the same distance.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: remember to keep transitions smooth and don't overreach with any stage to ensure balance and efficiency.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: being committed to all-out effort with each attempt will achieve the jumper’s best result.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: advising a partner will guide them to perform a technically sound approach and jump with maximal distance.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils often fail to get enough distance in the middle step phase of the triple jump and it is much shorter then the other two phases causing them to lose distance.
body: Help pupils to understand that ideally the distance covered in each phase will be similar. It might seem counterintuitive but the short step is often due to the hop stage being too long and we need to seek balance between all three stages.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: high jump requires a curved approach to build up speed and momentum.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: high jumpers take off from the outside foot by driving their knee and arm nearest the bar up and over.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: centrifugal force is generated using a curved run up to generate momentum.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: repeated practice and mental rehearsal builds confidence to execute a powerdul drive almost ignoring the bar.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: supportive feedback to peers on strengths and areas for improvement in jump technique requires sensitivity.

title: approach
body: the first phase of the long jump in which momentum is created in preparation for the jump
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: sending the shot requires an explosive ‘corkscrew’ sequence from knee to hips to chest.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: sit the shot in the fingers to ensure ‘clean palm, dirty neck’ and the elbow high to push behind the ball.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: self-talk in the moments prior to throwing can help increase focus and performance.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: commitment to executing the put with maximum force will ensure each thrower’s maximal result.

body: Connect: using good communication when helping a peer to improve technical errors will increase their chance of success.

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils often throw the shot by leading with the elbow rather than push it with the elbow following behind the shot, which can sometimes lead to pain and injury, especially to the wrist.
body: Emphasise the need to push the shot by extending the arm and not trying to bring the shot behind the head to throw. Replace shot with lighter weighted balls (medicine) if necessary to avoid injury while the technique is being learned.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: releasing the discus off the index finger last will give it the spin it needs to travel farther.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: use a self-talk countdown technique during the preparation phase to focus on timing the throw.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: confidence is built through repeated throws of the discus and acting on feedback.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils will grip the discus by wrapping their fingers and thumb around the edges to prevent it from slipping out or dropping it.

body: There are two main types of muscle contraction: isotonic (moving) and isometric (static).
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When the body is in a fixed position, but the muscle is contracting, it is known as an isometric (static) contraction.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Isotonic concentric contraction is the shortening of a muscle under tension.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Isotonic eccentric contraction is the lengthening of a muscle under tension
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: isotonic
body: muscle contraction that either shortens (concentric) or lengthens (eccentric)
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: isometric
body: muscle contraction where the length of the muscle does not alter. The contraction is constant.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: concentric
body: shortening of a muscle when it contracts
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: eccentric
body: lengthening of a muscle when it contracts
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A muscle will always change length when it contracts.
body: A muscle pulls on a bone to create movement. However, occasionally, if the movement is static, the muscle is still contracting and under tension but not changing length. This is known as isometric muscle contraction.

body: Move: receiving a ball safely with one or two hands requires moving our body towards the ball to keep it under control.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: keeping possession of the ball requires us to execute a variety of accurate passes.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: knowing that we have to pass the ball within 3 seconds requires decision making.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: focus and composure before every pass helps improve accuracy.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)
