body: a short pass in a crowded area that hits the ground once
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: overhead pass
body: a two handed pass thrown from above the head to outwit a player marking the ball
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accuracy
body: being correct and precise
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Power is more important than accuracy.
body: Accuracy is crucial to keep the ball within possession of your team so you have more opportunities to score.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: accelerating after a fake step in the opposite direction helps to get past a defender.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: dribbling with bent knees and a low body position maintains balance and allows for agile changes in direction.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: passing or shooting the ball before the fourth step/dribble will not break the travelling rule.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: it takes time to reset muscle memory when learning that you can take 3 steps while carrying the ball.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: using good communication and eye contact with teammates enables greater success at keeping possession.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a quick, fake movement (with the body or ball) used to trick a defender and create space to pass, move or shoot.

body: a player suddenly changes the direction of their dribble
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: bouncing a ball, holding it and bouncing the ball again
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: if a player does not pass or shoot the ball before taking the fourth step
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Dribbling is always the best option to move with the ball.
body: While dribbling can be helpful to gain ground up the court, it can slow down the game, whereas passing can often be faster and more efficient at breaking through a defence.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: using varied shots and angles creates unpredictability and increases the chances of scoring.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: shooting on the move allows players to maintain momentum and evade defenders.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: going into the ‘D’ is only permitted after the ball has been released.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: it takes confidence to jump or shoot while unstable, trusting your ability despite the lack of balance.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: having awareness of where the goalkeeper is improves the accuracy of scoring.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a shooting technique performed while the players feet are in the air
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: the various positions and directions from which a player can shoot at the goal to optimise their chance of scoring
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: when a player shoots the ball while falling or after losing balance, typically to avoid a defender’s block
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Players are not allowed in the D apart from the goalkeeper.
body: If you land in the goal area (the D) after taking a shot, the goal will still count as long as the ball was released before you entered the area. However, if you enter the goal area during regular play, possession is awarded to the opposing team.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: raising your arms as an opponent releases the ball, increases chances of blocking the ball and gaining possession.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: firm body position with a wide stance is crucial for effectively screening an opponent to control their movement.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: using your torso to block a player will not impede the obstruction rule but holding or pulling is prohibited.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: using your body to control your opposition’s movement takes confidence and assertiveness.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: coordinating with teammates to ensure they recognise the screen helps to exploit the space successfully.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a blocking move by an attacking player to free up a teammate
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: block
body: To block something is to stop it from moving or having an effect.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: closely guarding our opponent to prevent them from receiving the ball or from passing the ball to others
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Screening can be used by attackers to 'screen' or block defenders to allow an attacking teammate more space to move or score.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: passing the ball quickly from one side of the court to another makes it hard for defenders to reposition quickly.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: incorporating moves like crossing into an attacking play can confuse defenders, opening up opportunities to score.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: responding to how the opposition has positioned themselves utilises decision making and tactical awareness.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: taking a pause to use the width of the court in attack requires focus and thinking to outwit the defenders.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: communicating effectively with teammates before a tactical move is played avoids confusion.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: an imaginary line that divides the court vertically into 3 sections
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: crossing
body: players interchanging position to confuse defenders and open up shooting options
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: When attacking, it is always best to just dribble or step and pass the ball straight up the court.
body: Sometimes to create more space, a flat pass across the width of the pitch or a crossover move can be used to spread, reposition or confuse defenders which can be more successful at enabling a teammate to get through the gap that is created and score.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: to score more goals than our opponents we have to accurately time passes and movement to support the ball carrier.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Move: when our team loses possession, we need to react quickly to be ready to defend and stop the attack.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Think: reflecting on our performance ensures we understand how we can adapt our performance to keep improving.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Feel: always supporting our teammates to help them improve regardless of the score demonstrates integrity.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Connect: utilising playing positions to work with other members of the team in attack and defence shows teamwork.
attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: attacking

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A physical education lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils make simple ball handling mistakes due to rushing.

title: Pupils think a defensive player must catch the ball outright on initial contact from a shot.

body: The cardiac cycle consists of two main phases: diastole and systole.

body: Systole is the phase when the heart chambers contract and pump blood out at high pressure.

body: Monoclonal antibodies recognise a specific target, such as an antigen or other biological molecule.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Monoclonal antibodies are produced by combining a lymphocyte and a tumour cell to produce a hybridoma.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The hybridoma divides to make many copies of this single clone, which make monoclonal antibodies.

body: Monoclonal antibodies are used to detect pathogen antigens & molecules associated with pregnancy, blood clots & cancer.

body: Monoclonal antibodies can be attached to radioactive and toxic substances to treat diseased cells, e.g. tumour cells.

title: Monoclonal antibodies can act as a 'magic bullet' to deliver medication to certain cells.
body: The human body is complex and therapies using monoclonal antibodies have had some serious side effects. New treatments should always be treated with caution.

body: All organisms are made up of one or more cells.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Multicellular organisms grow by making new cells.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: New cells are made when existing cells divide by mitosis.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Specialised cells in multicellular organisms (including humans and plants) have shapes, sizes and structures that are adapted for the jobs the cells do.

body: The genetic material of all organisms is made of DNA, wound up into structures called chromosomes.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Sections of chromosomes are called genes, which store instructions for making proteins (including enzymes).
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The proteins that are made are used to build other structures and control chemical reactions.

body: An early animal embryo is made of unspecialised cells; these are embryonic stem cells.

body: As an animal develops into an adult, some cells remain unspecialised; these are adult stem cells.

body: Adult stem cells can differentiate to become most but not all types of cells in the animal’s body.

body: Plants have unspecialised cells called meristem cells, which are located in the stem and the tips of roots and shoots.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Meristem cells in roots and shoots divide and differentiate to enable roots and shoots to grow longer and wider.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Meristem cells in the shoots also divide and differentiate to make leaves and flowers.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Meristem cells in the stem and roots also divide and differentiate to make tissues such as xylem and phloem.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Meristem tissue can be used to produce clones for crops or to protect endangered species.

body: Plants are multicellular organisms – they are made up of millions of living cells.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Plants do not have a circulatory system (they do not have blood, blood vessels or a heart).
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cells need to be supplied with nutrients including carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and water for growth and repair.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cells need to be supplied with oxygen and glucose for cellular respiration to provide energy for life processes.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cells with chloroplasts need to be supplied with carbon dioxide and water for photosynthesis.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Particles of substances move by diffusion into and out of cells through selectively-permeable cell membranes.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Exchange surfaces are adapted to maximise the surface area for diffusion of particles across membranes.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In humans, the circulatory system transports essential substances around the body and minimises the distance they have to diffuse so cells can be supplied quickly.

title: Many pupils believe that in order to determine a population size within a habitat, all organisms within a habitat have to be counted.
body: Populations can be estimated using sampling techniques. As long as a sample size is large enough, it will provide a reliable estimate of the population size. Pupils should understand that counting all individuals in a habitat is very difficult to do.
